Quantum resistance paradox of low-dimensional superfluids

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 50 min read (9963 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nature

⏱️ ~50 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Resistance in standard conductors decreases with increasing cross-section.
  • The Landau model provides a powerful framework for understanding many phases of matter through the lens of spontaneous symmetry breaking6,7.
  • For example, in a voltage-biased superconducting wire, the applied voltage continuously winds the superconducting phase, causing an increase of the phase gradient between the contacts.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Resistance in standard conductors decreases with increasing cross-section. Yet, in low-dimensional superconductors and superfluids, residual resistance arises from topological fluctuations of the order parameter, manifesting as phase slips in one-dimensional (1D) and vortices in two-dimensional (2D) systems. How resistance and dissipation evolve as geometry interpolates between these regimes remains an open question. This evolution is masked in solid-state experiments by disorder, impurities and geometric imperfections1,2,3, and poses theoretical challenges due to competing dissipative processes and pronounced finite-size effects. Here, we use a defect-free unitary Fermi gas in a digitally programmable transport geometry to isolate geometric effects on superfluid dissipation and discover a paradox: in the crossover from one dimension to two dimensions, the resistance reaches a minimum. There, widening a channel increases its resistance. Narrower, quasi-1D channels show dissipation described by Langer–Ambegaokar–McCumber–Halperin theory of phase slips4. In this regime, varying the channel width yields the predicted exponential scaling of the activation factor over many orders of magnitude. Wider, quasi-2D channels show dissipation consistent with phase-slip events described by a finite-size vortex model5. The minimal dissipation in the dimensional crossover reflects a transition in the dominant dissipative mechanism, with both 1D and 2D events simultaneously suppressed. Our measurements suggest a route to minimizing dissipation in superconducting devices and provide a benchmark for theoretical efforts aimed at describing the dimensional crossover.

The Landau model provides a powerful framework for understanding many phases of matter through the lens of spontaneous symmetry breaking6,7. In superfluids and superconductors, this breaking manifests in the emergence of a macroscopic condensate that exhibits long-range phase coherence. This coherence is ultimately responsible for properties such as dissipationless transport8,9, the Josephson effect10, and in the case of superconductivity the Meissner effect11. Although relatively robust in bulk systems, in lower-dimensional systems, the enhanced effect of fluctuations—and in particular topological defects—can suppress this long-range phase coherence and govern superfluid transport4,12.

For example, in a voltage-biased superconducting wire, the applied voltage continuously winds the superconducting phase, causing an increase of the phase gradient between the contacts. The supercurrent, proportional to this gradient, would grow without bound unless intermittent phase fluctuations relax the accumulated gradient. By relaxing the gradient, the fluctuations dissipate energy, thereby causing a resistance3,13. The characteristics of the fluctuations and their corresponding resistance depend on the dimensionality of the setup as follows.

In a recent development, in one-dimensional (1D) wires, discrete relaxation events known as phase slips dominate the dynamics. Microscopically, a phase slip occurs when the magnitude of the superconducting order parameter is transiently and locally suppressed over a healing length ξ. Where the amplitude vanishes, the phase is ill-defined, allowing for phase jumps of 2π. As the order parameter recovers, the wire returns to a state with a uniform amplitude but a reduced phase gradient4 (Fig. 1a, top row).

a, Dissipation in a narrow, quasi-1D channel occurs because of phase slips, in which a depletion of the order parameter allows for a relaxation of the phase gradient and kinetic energy (top row). The corresponding phase (colour-coded) evolution of a phase slip in a narrow channel is plotted in the central row. In a wide, quasi-2D channel, dissipation is governed by vortex–antivortex pairs traversing the channel (bottom row). b, A transport channel of programmable width connects two superfluid reservoirs (blue). The channel is formed by two repulsive beams (green and orange), one of which is tunable by a DMD.

Industry observers note that in two-dimensional (2D) geometries, such as thin films, dissipation instead arises from the nucleation and motion of topological defects known as vortices. A vortex is a point-like singularity of the phase around which the phase winds by 2π, with a small core in which the amplitude is suppressed. Driven by a current, vortices move across the film and dissipate energy. Each time a vortex traverses the sample, the phase difference between the contacts relaxes by 2π. Repeated vortex crossings generate a finite voltage and hence an effective resistance14,15 (Fig. 1a, bottom row). In intermediate, thin-strip geometries, both vortex flow and phase slips may contribute to dissipation.

Previous studies included experiments on superconducting rings16; Dayem-bridge nanowires17,18,19,20; Bose–Einstein condensates in dumbbell21,22, cylindrical23 or toroidal geometries24; optical lattices25,26; and fermionic Josephson junctions27,28,29. These previous studies have explored various facets of phase-slip and vortex physics, including direct imaging of vortices28,30,31,32, the Berezinskii–Kosterlitz–Thouless phase transition33 and the recent observation of Shapiro steps in atomic Josephson junctions34,35. However, the experimental challenge of isolating and characterizing geometric or dimensional effects on dissipation remains unresolved.

With the rise of quantum simulation of devices based on highly controllable ultracold atomic gases36,37, it is now possible to shed new light on how these dissipative processes emerge in quantum systems.

In this work, we use ultracold, strongly interacting fermions in a two-terminal configuration to study nonlinear transport through a digitally programmable channel. The optically shaped channel can be reproducibly tuned from a quasi-1D to a quasi-2D geometry, providing a platform ideally suited for probing the influence of geometry on fluctuation-driven dissipation in the absence of defects or impurities.

According to recent reports, in the narrow, 1D channel limit, we identify signatures of phase slips, in agreement with the Langer–Ambegaokar–McCumber–Halperin (LAMH) theory4,38,39. In particular, we observe the predicted exponential suppression of the LAMH activation factor over many orders of magnitude on widening the channel. For even larger widths, the system crosses over to a 2D regime in which dissipation is dominated by vortices, as indicated by the observed power-law dependence of the current–voltage characteristics predicted for vortex dynamics.

Beyond establishing these limiting behaviours, our measurements provide a direct window into the crossover between 1D and 2D transport, a regime in which analytical modelling is challenging. It is in this crossover that widening the channel paradoxically increases its resistance. More broadly, our results highlight the utility of ultracold atomic superfluids as a platform for quantum simulation of nonequilibrium transport.

In a recent development, we prepare a balanced mixture of the lowest and third-lowest hyperfine states of fermionic 6Li in the unitary regime. A total of 2N = 2.7 ± 0.1 × 105 atoms are cooled to T/TF = 0.144 ± 0.007, where N denotes the number of atom pairs, TF denotes the Fermi temperature, and the errors in both quantities denote the uncertainties due to shot-to-shot fluctuations. The temperature corresponds to T/TC ≈ 0.7, where TC ≈ 0.2TF denotes the critical temperature40. The atoms are confined in a cigar-shaped, harmonic trap with trapping frequencies (νx, νy, νz) = (222 ± 7, 28.1 ± 0.1, 195 ± 5) Hz.

As shown in Fig. 1a, a repulsive TEM0,1 beam, propagating in the x-direction, is aligned with the trap centre. It divides the atomic cloud into two reservoirs, separated by a quasi-2D transport region that is 51 ± 1 μm long and provides confinement of ν2D = 10.46 ± 0.09 kHz along z. Within the central 27 ± 0.5 μm of this plane, the atoms are further confined in the x-direction to a channel of variable width w. The channel is defined by a repulsive beam propagating along z, shaped by a digital micromirror device (DMD). It enables reproducible tunability of w from 0.9 ± 0.5 μm to 19.8 ± 0.5 μm, in which the uncertainty is dominated by and calculated from the resolution limit of our projection system (numerical aperture = 0.53, λ = 532 nm). Note that given the dimensions of our setup, we are not in the Josephson regime (see Methods, ‘No Josephson oscillations’). A third, attractive Gaussian beam (not shown) illuminates the transport channel and its connections to the reservoirs, locally increasing the degeneracy. A more detailed description of this effect as well as of the overall setup can be found in ref. 41.

Recent findings suggest that at time t = 0, we prepare a relative atom-pair imbalance between the two reservoirs, ΔN/N = (Nl − Nr)/(Nl + Nr), where Nl,r denote the number of atom pairs in the left and right reservoirs. An initial imbalance of ΔN/N ≈ 0.1 relaxes through an approximately constant initial current, followed by damped oscillations of the imbalance. The discharge is distinctly non-exponential, indicating a nonlinear response. The damping, and in particular its dependence on the channel width w, carries information about the underlying microscopic mechanisms.

Sources indicate that the key data of our measurement series are shown in Fig. 2a. We record transport traces for w between 0.9 ± 0.5 μm and 19.8 ± 0.5 μm. As w increases, the magnitude of the initial current increases, which manifests in a steeper initial slope. Concurrently, both the oscillation frequency and amplitude grow. The frequency rises from just below 10 Hz to approximately 18 Hz (see also Extended Data Fig. 1). For the narrowest channel (w = 0.9 ± 0.5 μm), the oscillation amplitude is comparable to the noise floor and barely resolved. By contrast, for the widest channel (w = 19.8 ± 0.5 μm), the amplitude reaches ΔN/N ≈ 0.06.

According to recent reports, a, Atom transport (imbalance ΔN/N as a function of time t) of a unitary Fermi gas through channels of increasing width shows distinctively changing dissipation characteristics. The data are compared with fitted phase slip (LAMH) and vortex models. The models both describe the TNR in the circuit (b), capturing either phase slips or vortices. The LAMH model fits narrow channels, whereas the vortex model fits wide channels. The measurements for different channel widths are vertically offset for clarity. The statistical uncertainties of the measurements (typically four to five measurements per data point) are smaller than the marker size. c, A quality-of-fit \({\chi }_{\nu }^{2}\) analysis substantiates the change of the dominant model apparent in a.

Recent findings suggest that the damping exhibits a non-monotonic dependence on w. At longer transport times (for example, t = 0.3 s), the remaining oscillation amplitude reaches a maximum for intermediate channel widths (see also Fig. 4). These signals suggest distinct dissipative mechanisms in the narrow and wide channel limits, which we analyse quantitatively below.

The general characteristics of the dynamics can be understood as arising from the interplay between the potential energy stored in the reservoirs, the kinetic energy inside the channel and the dissipative processes we want to investigate. To study these dissipative processes, we model our system with an equivalent RLC circuit shown in Fig. 2b. We first characterize the capacitance and inductance of the circuit to subsequently infer the dissipative (resistive) processes by fitting the dynamics of the circuit to the measurements. The capacitances, inductance and resistance in the circuit model correspond to the compressibility of the atomic reservoirs, the inertia of the atoms and the dissipative processes in the channel, respectively. We explore these elements in the following starting with the capacitors. As the model circuit features two capacitors in series, each with a capacitance C, the effective capacitance of the circuit is Ceff = C/2. The compressibility κeff of the gas allows to quantify this equivalent capacitance Ceff (potential energy per atom pair displaced from equilibrium) through \(\frac{1}{2}{(\Delta N/2)}^{2}/{\kappa }_{\mathrm{eff}}=\Delta {E}_{\mathrm{pot}}\equiv \frac{1}{2}{(\Delta N/2)}^{2}/{C}_{\mathrm{eff}}\). We measured the compressibility of our sample (Methods, ‘Derivation of the reservoir capacitance’) to find hCeff = 15.8 ± 0.5 s, where h is Planck’s constant. Next we quantify the inductance. To do so, we assume all channels have box-like potentials. A charge-neutral atom-pair current I carries a kinetic energy Ekin that depends on w. We define the inductance of our systems using \({E}_{{\rm{kin}}}\equiv \frac{1}{2}L{I}^{2}.\) We developed a model that predicts a functional dependence.

In a recent development, (Methods, ‘Derivation of the inductance’). By analysing the oscillation frequencies observed in our measurements and noting that in a weakly damped circuit, the frequencies are given by \(\omega (w)\approx 1/\sqrt{L(w){C}_{\mathrm{eff}}}\), we find ℓc/h = 3.01 ± 0.03 × 10−5 μm s and Lres/h = 3.06 ± 0.04 × 10−6 s. Although the details are provided in the Supplementary Information, here we state that the first term in equation (1) captures the kinetic energy in the channel, whereas the second term accounts for the kinetic energy in the reservoirs.

According to recent reports, phase slips and vortices dissipate the kinetic energy of the current into heat. So, they effectively act as a topological nonlinear resistor (TNR). With L and C determined, the resistance R remains the sole unknown component in our circuit. Owing to the nature of phase slips, R is topological and nonlinear, meaning it depends not only on the geometry but also on the current.

Showing how R depends on geometry, in particular in relation to the length scale given by ξ ≈ 1.2 μm (Methods, ‘Estimate of ξ’), reveals the nature of the underlying dissipative processes. To do so, we fit the width-dependent resistance R(w) in the equations of motion of an RLC circuit (derived in Methods, ‘RLC circuit modelling and fitting’).

For narrow, quasi-1D channels (w ≱ 2ξ), we expect the system to be in the phase slip regime. The LAMH model predicts4.

According to recent reports, defined using R = V/I, where R0 is the characteristic resistance, w0 is the characteristic width, and I0 = 2kBT/h, where kB is the Boltzmann’s constant and T is the temperature. The exponential suppression of R with w reflects the thermally activated phase-slip rate scaling with \(\varGamma \propto \exp (-\Delta F/({k}_{{\rm{B}}}T))\) (ref. 18), where the free energy barrier for phase slips is ΔF ∝ w. The sinh(I/I0) term can intuitively be understood as follows: at small |I/I0| ≪ 1, phase slips occur in both directions with roughly equal probability; as the bias increases slightly, phase slips that relax the current become more probable. For large |I/I0| ≫ 1, sinh(I/I0) ≈ exp(I/I0)/2. reflecting the local destabilization of the superfluid and the resulting exponential increase in the phase-slip probability.

Using our predetermined C and L(w), we determine R0 and w0 by fitting them simultaneously to the measurements of our four narrowest channels (Methods, ‘RLC circuit modelling and fitting’). Assuming that the LAMH model can be used to describe our system, a simultaneous fit to multiple channel widths provides a robust extraction of the model parameters but enforces the predicted exponential suppression of RLAMH with w. We find R0/h = 102.3±0.2 and w0 = 49.7(6) nm, where the errors denote the uncertainties of the fit. The resulting fits (shown in Fig. 2a) largely capture the dynamics for channels with a width up to w = 2.5 μm. This is quantified by \(\mathrm{NRMSE}\,=\) \(\sqrt{{\sum }_{i}{({m}_{i}-{f}_{i})}^{2}/N}/({m}_{\max }-{m}_{\min }) < 0.06\), where mi and fi denote the measured and fitted imbalances, respectively, and mmax − mmin is the measured signal range. However, the \({\chi }_{\nu }^{2}\) analysis \(({\chi }_{\nu }^{2}\lesssim 9)\) shown in Fig. 2c suggests additional systematic effects beyond the very small statistical uncertainties of the measurements (typically on the level of 0.004). These systematic effects could originate from the approximation of modelling the channel with a box-like potential or the attractive beam illuminating the channel locally increasing the temperature. Outside the validity range of the model, the quality of the fits degrades noticeably, failing to capture the phase of the oscillations and underestimating their damping.

In a second step, we validate the choice of the LAMH model by fitting RLAMH(w) to each curve individually. In contrast to the simultaneous fit, these individual fits do not enforce the predicted scaling RLAMH(w) and therefore provide an independent test of whether the scaling is present in the data. Within the validity regime of the model, the individual fits reproduce the predicted exponential scaling over many orders of magnitude, as shown in Fig. 3a.

a, The fitted phase-slip resistance RLAMH(w), for narrow channels, shows the exponential suppression with width, as predicted by LAMH theory. b, The fitted vortex resistivity ρv(w), for wide channels, shows the predicted power law. Inside the crossover region (2–4ξ), that is, outside the validity range of the models, both scalings break down (Methods, ‘Breakdown of scaling laws’). Note that a and b display different quantities (resistance compared with resistivity) characterizing different regimes (1D compared with 2D) and are therefore not intended to be compared across the dimensional crossover. The error bars represent the error of the fit.

In a recent development, this is the first main finding of this paper. Compared with RLAMH(w), the total resistance R(I, w) apparent in the measurements (Fig. 2a) varies much less. As we initialize a fixed potential bias in our system, the exponential geometric suppression (R ∝ exp(−w/w0)) approximately cancels the current-induced exponential enhancement (R ∝ sinh(I/I0) ≈ exp(I/I0)/2). This allows RLAMH to be inferred over a wide range—more than 10 decades—while only exploring a relatively modest dynamic range of R. Importantly, the observed scaling of RLAMH(w) is contained within the data itself and is not just an artefact of the choice of the model. This becomes evident when the model is applied outside its validity regime, where the scaling breaks down immediately (Methods, ‘Breakdown of scaling laws’).

In quasi-2D channels (w ≳ 4ξ), phase slips become energetically unfavourable, as their activation energy increases exponentially with w. Instead, dissipation is expected to be governed by vortex flow. Owing to the vortices, we expect to see a power-law dependence in the pair-current density J:.

where J0 = I0/ξ. A derivation, building on the results of ref. 5, is provided in the Methods, ‘Vortices in a finite width’. By fitting α and \({\widetilde{R}}_{0}\) simultaneously to the data of our four widest channels (Methods, ‘RLC circuit modelling and fitting’), we find \(\alpha =1.98\pm 0.04,{\mathop{R}\limits^{ \sim }}_{0}/h=1{0}^{-4.79\pm 0.07}\). As apparent from Fig. 2a, this model captures the dynamics for channels in the 2D regime (NRMSE ≱ 0.06). In these cases, \({\chi }_{\nu }^{2}\lesssim 4\). Note that the vortex model does not contain an explicit temperature dependence, and for wide channels, the box-potential approximation is safer compared with narrow channels. Apart from these statistical tests, we validate our model by fixing α to its global fit value but fitting ρv to each individual curve. Within the validity range of the model, these individual fits agree with the predicted power-law ρv ∝ wα−1 (Fig. 3b). This scaling is the second main finding of the paper. The scaling breaks down outside the validity regime of the model (Methods, ‘Breakdown of scaling laws’), providing evidence that the observed scaling is a feature of the data, not a mere artefact of the enforced power law R ∝ Jα−1. When approaching the dimensional crossover w ≱ 4ξ, while still largely capturing the dynamics, the model begins to slightly but systematically underestimate the amplitude of the oscillations at long times. Presumably, because the approximation of sufficiently large w used in the derivation of R(J) ceases to hold (Methods, ‘Vortices in a finite width’). The eventual breakdown of the vortex model at w ≈ 4ξ marks the end of the 2D regime: the vortex model should be valid only when vortex–antivortex pairs are available as excitations. As each vortex has a radius of ξ, such an excitation requires w ≳ 4ξ. This leaves a gap between the validity ranges of the phase slip and the vortex model, in which neither model provides a microscopically satisfactory description. In this gap, there is a dimensional crossover, in which both phase slips and vortices compete.

The underdamped oscillations allow us to characterize dissipation in our system using only a few basic assumptions, while staying agnostic to the dissipation mechanism. This is particularly useful to analyse the dimensional crossover, in which neither the phase-slip nor the vortex model provide a satisfactory microscopical description. We split the total energy Etot into a potential (capacitive) energy EC and a kinetic (inductive) energy EL. We assume Etot = EC(ΔN) + EL(I, w) with EC ∝ ΔN2 and EL(I = 0, w) = 0. For each channel width w, we extract the times ti,w at which ΔN(t = ti, w) reaches an extremum and thus I ≈ 0. There, the system has minimal inductive energy (EL ≈ 0) and maximal capacitive energy. The fraction of the initial energy remaining in the system is then given by.

Recent findings suggest that the remaining energy as a function of time and channel width is shown in Fig. 4. The plot is obtained by cubic interpolation between the measured points, performed linearly in time and logarithmically in width.

Industry observers note that the remaining energy in the oscillator paradoxically varies non-monotonically as a function of the channel width w. For a given time after the initial decay, the maximum appears in the crossover region, near w = 4 μm ≈ 3ξ, in which phase slips and vortices are suppressed but competing. The crosses mark the measurement points (typically four to five measurements per cross) between which we interpolate. We estimate the individual data points to have a typical positive bias of 0.5% and a statistical uncertainty smaller than 2% (Methods, ‘Error estimation’).

According to recent reports, for a fixed width, the energy decays over time, reflecting dissipation. At any given time t > 0.15 s, Et(w)/E0 varies non-monotonically with the channel width, exhibiting a clear maximum near w ≈ 3ξ, corresponding to a minimal effective resistance. We call this deviation from the expected monotonicity the ‘quantum resistance paradox’ and consider it the third and last main finding of this paper. Note that the activation energy for phase slips increases exponentially with channel width, whereas vortex–antivortex pairs require sufficiently wide channels to form. The observed non-monotonicity thus suggests a transition in the underlying dissipation mechanism and a crossover from 1D to 2D physics.

We have investigated atom transport between two bulk superfluids through channels across different dimensional regimes and observed distinct behaviours. In narrow, quasi-1D channels, our data are in agreement with those of the LAMH model. We infer the geometric suppression of the phase slips by many orders of magnitude, providing the first experimental confirmation of the predicted geometric scaling. For wide, quasi-2D channels, dissipation is captured by a vortex flow model. The borders of the 1D and 2D regimes appear close to the theoretically expected length scale. A measurement of energy decay, agnostic to microscopic details, provides further evidence for a transition in the dissipation mechanism for channels of intermediate width, which paradoxically exhibit the least energy loss. These findings not only suggest routes for optimizing energy transport in mesoscopic devices but also provide a benchmark for theoretical efforts to describe the delicate phase-slip and vortex-flow mechanisms in the dimensional crossover in superfluids and superconductors42,43,44.

Our setup is analogous to an RLC circuit with the mapping presented in Extended Data Table 1.

In a recent development, the procedures for determining the capacitance C and the inductance L are described in sections ‘Derivation of the reservoir capacitance’ and ‘Derivation of the inductance’. Here, we derive the governing equations and provide additional details on the fitting procedure used to determine R, as presented in the main text.

The total number of atoms in each reservoir is measured directly using absorption images of both hyperfine states (|1⟩ and |3⟩), taken in rapid succession. To determine the total number of pairs in each reservoir Nl,r, we use both measurements, as this reduces statistical uncertainty. Specifically, \({N}_{{\rm{l}},{\rm{r}}}=({N}_{{\rm{l}},{\rm{r}};|1\rangle }+{N}_{{\rm{l}},{\rm{r}};|3\rangle })/2\), where \({N}_{{\rm{l}},{\rm{r}};|i\rangle }\) denotes the number of atoms in the left and right reservoirs in state |i⟩. However, the second image (state |3⟩) highlights a cloud that has absorbed some energy from the first imaging pulse and is therefore slightly distorted. To avoid systematic effects from this distortion on C and T, we use only the image of the lowest hyperfine state (|1⟩) to extract the compressibility and temperature of the cloud, assuming these are identical for both states. We verified that our preparation is equivalent for both states by inverting the imaging sequence. We describe our system in terms of pairs and report C, L and R for pairs and pair currents, respectively.

It has been revealed that as shown in Fig. 2b, our RLC circuit consists of two capacitors (reservoirs) in series. We replace these two capacitors C by an effective capacitance Ceff = C/2. With this replacement, we obtain a standard RLC series circuit with an initially charged capacitor but no externally applied voltage.

Applying Kirchhoff’s voltage law and charge conservation, we find.

Using the mapping Q ↔ ΔN/2 and Ceff = C/2, we obtain.

Phase slips and vortices induce nonlinear resistances, so R = R(I) or R = R(J), where I and J denote the pair current and pair-current density, respectively. Depending on the model, we use.

Equations (9) and (10) are then integrated numerically.

Experimentally, transport is initiated by ramping down a blue-detuned beam that blocks the channel. A sudden quench of this beam slightly perturbs the reservoirs, so we instead ramp it down over 10 ms. This introduces an unknown initial condition I(t = 0). For each curve, we fit I(t = 0) ∈ [0, Iavg], where Iavg is the average current during the initial decay (before oscillations). To avoid giving undue weight to the first measured point, we fit ΔNfit(t = 0) ∈ [0.8, 1.2] ⋅ ΔNmeasured(t = 0). These bounds are necessary to prevent the models from ignoring the initial decay outside their validity regime. In particular, this is the case for the LAMH model when fitting data of wide channels, where only a few points represent the initial dynamics.

For numerical stability, R0 and \({\widetilde{R}}_{0}\) are fitted on a logarithmic scale, whereas α and w0 are fitted linearly.

Finally, we discuss the fitting weights. Each configuration (t, w) has five measurements. Points with preparation errors (low atom number) are excluded, typically leaving four to five measurements per point and occasionally three. The experimental standard deviation is calculated for each configuration individually. We assume that for a given w, the uncertainty is independent of t. To prevent the fit from being dominated by points with unrealistically small uncertainties, both the fitting and the \({\chi }_{\nu }^{2}\) calculations replace individual error bars with the median error bar of all the data sharing w.

The \({\chi }_{\nu }^{2}\) analysis shown in Fig. 2c is performed as follows. The uncertainty of the measured points is assumed to be identical for all points belonging to a specific channel width. For each channel width, the model is fitted, either with 2.5 effective degrees of freedom (R0, w0, ΔN0, I0 or \({\widetilde{R}}_{0},\alpha ,\Delta {N}_{0},{I}_{0}\)), where the first two parameters are shared among four channels (2/4 = 0.5) if the channel participates in the global fit of the respective model, or two degrees of freedom (ΔN0, I0) otherwise. The reduced chi-squared is then calculated using \({\chi }_{\nu }^{2}=\frac{1}{n-m}\sum \frac{{({m}_{i}-{f}_{i})}^{2}}{{\sigma }^{2}}\), where mi are the measured values, fi the corresponding values fitted by the model, σ the uncertainty shared by all measurement points of a specific width, n the number of measured points and m = 2.5 or m = 2 the number of effectively fitted degrees of freedom.

It has been revealed that we discuss how the fitted models are affected by the various sources of systematic uncertainty. Specifically, we investigate how systematic uncertainties in the capacitance C, the channel width w and the temperature T affect the quality of the model fits and the inferred parameters RLAMH and α.

Assume that the true physical capacitance \(\widetilde{C}\) differs from the calculated value (see section ‘Derivation of the reservoir capacitance’) by a factor γ, such that \(C=\gamma \widetilde{C}\). In our analysis, the effective inductance L is determined (see section ‘Derivation of the inductance’) before fitting the resistance by analysing the underdamped, multi-period oscillations of the system. Owing to the observation of multiple periods, the frequency can be measured with good accuracy and precision. A systematic shift γ ≠ 1 would therefore result in an inverse scaling of the extracted inductance curve, \(L\approx \widetilde{L}/\gamma \), where \(\widetilde{L}\) represents the true physical inductance. Inspecting the underlying equation of motion of the circuit (equation (2)) demonstrates that the extracted resistance scales identically with this factor (R ∝ 1/γ). This uniform rescaling by 1/α can be absorbed in the prefactor R0 or \({\widetilde{R}}_{0}\), leaving the quality of the fits, scalings, the inferred dynamic ranges and the geometric suppression constant w0 entirely unaffected.

The geometric potential landscape is projected onto the atoms using a DMD. Although physical pixel spacing and optical demagnification ratio are known accurately, the primary source of spatial uncertainty stems from the finite resolution of the imaging optics. The finite resolution effectively blurs the repulsive potential walls of the channel. Consequently, having to choose where to define the sharp boundaries of the model (spaced by w) within this blurred profile introduces a systematic uncertainty Δw.

Importantly, this geometric uncertainty of roughly 0.5 μm is expected to be shared across all channel configurations and does not affect each channel independently of the others. For channels in the 1D regime, the initial discharge through the narrowest channels is characterized by an extended period of nearly constant current in which inertial forces are negligible (∣L dI/dt∣ ≪ |RI|). In this regime, the system behaves predominantly as a nonlinear RC circuit, approximately decoupling the resistance fit from the precise value of L. Then, a uniform translation of w by Δw alters the resistances by a constant factor. For the LAMH model, \(R(w+\Delta w)\propto \exp (-\Delta w/{w}_{0})\). Similarly to the capacitance error, this effect is entirely absorbed by a re-normalization of the global prefactor R0, preserving both the dynamic range of RLAMH and its slope set by w0. The relatively high value of \({\chi }_{\nu }^{2}\) for the LAMH model might be caused by the experiment that violates the assumption of box-like channel potentials. For the channels in the 2D regime, Δw/w ≪ 1, so we expect systematic effects caused by Δw ≠ 0 to be small and the approximation of modelling the channels as box-like to be safe.

Although we calibrated our measurements with the thermodynamic reference point of Bose–Einstein condensation, our measured atom-pair numbers and temperatures (see sections ‘High-saturation imaging’ and ‘Thermodynamic state extraction by 2D equation of state fitting’) might be subject to systematic errors. An error in the inferred pair-number \(N=\gamma \widetilde{N}\), where N is the inferred particle number and \(\widetilde{N}\) is the physical particle number, would force a corresponding shift in C, thereby rescaling L and R as discussed above. Moreover, it would rescale I. As the current enters the expression for the resistance in the vortex model only in the form of a power law, it would merely shift \(\widetilde{R}\) by a constant factor γ−α. Again, this constant factor would affect neither α, nor the quality of the vortex-model fits, nor the quality of its scaling law. As the vortex model does not contain an explicit temperature dependence, it is unaffected by potential systematic effects in T. For the LAMH model, the situation is different. The temperature enters the model explicitly through I0 = 2kBT/h. Variations in both N and T ultimately tie into the ratio I/I0. Because this ratio controls the degree of nonlinearity of the circuit, we can model their combined systematic impact by analysing variations in I0 alone.

The initial discharge of the narrowest channels is distinctly nonlinear (implying I ≫ I0), whereas the subsequent oscillations are approximately sinusoidal (implying I ≱ I0). Consequently, the ratio I/I0 is constrained by the geometric profile of the relaxation curves. However, systematic effects that affect the ratio I/I0 do also affect the quality of fit and the dynamic range of RLAMH. In general, if I/I0 is lowered (by decreasing I or increasing T), the circuit is less nonlinear and the dynamic range of RLAMH decreases, whereas an increase in the ratio has the opposite effect. Although the parameter I0 is constrained in the LAMH model, we performed additional fittings, where I0 was a global fit parameter, to effectively account for potential systematic errors in I or T. The best fits are achieved with I0,fit = 3.50(1)I0, reducing \({\chi }_{\nu }^{2}\) averaged over the five narrowest channels, by more than a factor of 2. A possible cause for this could be that the attractive Gaussian beam illuminating the channel locally heats the channel, thereby increasing I0. Note that this beam also increases the local degeneracy such that we would still expect the channel to be deeply degenerate. Although in the case of fitted I0, the dynamic range of RLAMH is reduced, it continues to span more than four orders of magnitude. The values are still in good agreement with the predicted exponential scaling.

In a recent development, for all channel widths except the narrowest one, we observe underdamped, long-lived oscillations. As these oscillations remain underdamped, the influence of the nonlinear resistance on the oscillation frequency is expected to be small. To extract the inductance of the channel for each width (except the narrowest one), we exclude the initial transient dynamics up to the first, global minimum occurring at a time t = t1,w. The remaining data are fitted with a damped sinusoidal function \({f}_{w}(t)={A}_{w}\exp (-(t-{t}_{1,w})/{\tau }_{w})\sin ({\omega }_{w}t+{\phi }_{{\rm{w}}})+\Delta {N}_{w,\mathrm{offset}},\) where Aw, τw, ωw, ϕw, and ΔNw,offset are fitting parameters. Small offsets |ΔNw,offset| < 0.018 account for potential alignment errors that cause the oscillations to centre around slightly nonzero values. Using the inferred effective capacitance Ceff of our circuit (see section ‘Derivation of the reservoir capacitance’), we determine the total inductance for a given channel width as \({L}_{w}=1/(({\omega }_{w}^{2}+{\tau }_{w}^{-2}){C}_{\mathrm{eff}})\approx 1/({\omega }_{w}^{2}C),\) where the approximation is equivalent to the result for an undamped LC circuit and holds for weakly damped circuits. Although the quantitative difference in our case is minute, we do include the τ-term capturing the effect of the resistance lowering the oscillation frequency of the RLC circuit. Note that for the wide channels in particular, fitting a damped sine to the oscillatory data is a pragmatic choice that allows for an approximation of the inductance, the signature of which is primarily contained in the frequency of the oscillation. Over extended periods of time, however, the damped sine and the dynamics of the vortex model would appear different, as the latter does not feature an exponentially decaying amplitude. This kinetic inductance Lw quantifies the kinetic energy associated with a given pair current I. Although the main contribution arises from the transport channel itself, there is also a residual contribution because of particle motion in the adjoining 2D and 3D regions, whose geometries are independent of the channel width. We therefore write \(L(w)={L}_{\mathrm{channel}}(w)+{L}_{\mathrm{res}}\). Assuming a constant particle density inside the channel, the mass of particles in the transport channel (M) scales with its width, M ∝ w. For a given current, the corresponding particle velocity in the channel thus scales inversely, \({v}_{\mathrm{channel}}\propto \frac{1}{w}\). Consequently, the kinetic energy associated with a fixed I scales as \({E}_{\mathrm{kin}}=M{v}_{\mathrm{channel}}^{2}/2\propto w{(1/w)}^{2}=1/w\), implying that Lchannel(w) ∝ 1/w. We therefore model the total inductance as.

It has been revealed that with fitting parameters ℓc and Lres. We find ℓc/h = 3.01(3) × 10−5 μm s and Lres/h = 3.06(4) × 10−6 s, where the uncertainties represent the standard errors of the fit. The measured inductances Lw and the fitted model are shown in Extended Data Fig. 1. The excellent agreement of the model with the data validates our model assumptions.

In a previous, comparable experimental setting, we estimated the atoms traversing a region of length d ≈ 3 μm in a time t ≈ 330 μs, resulting in an estimated atomic velocity of v ≈ 9 mm s−1 (ref. 48). As our channel is practically defect free, we assume that the atomic velocity is close to the critical velocity vc. So we estimate 4ξ ≈ 4ħ/(mvc) ≈ 5 μm (ref. 49).

It has been revealed that given the method with which we extract the energy ratio, two main sources of error are to be considered. The first one is the statistical noise of the measurement points. This directly translates into an uncertainty of the inferred energy ratio but also causes a systematic bias towards higher values, as only the extrema of the signals are considered. The second contribution comes from the finite sampling rate of the oscillations. This causes an uncertainty and a bias towards lower values, as the measured points do not sample the peaks exactly. To quantitatively assess their influence for all our measurements, we performed Monte Carlo simulations. Specifically, we sampled sinusoidal signals with the frequencies, amplitudes and dampings observed in the signals used for Fig. 4. We sampled these artificial signals with the sampling rates and statistical noise that occurred in the physical experiment. This simulation yielded the following insight: For the data presented in Fig. 4, the inferred energies have a typical positive bias of 0.5% and a standard deviation smaller than 2%.

Industry observers note that although several studies have reported on Josephson oscillations with seemingly similar measurements in comparable settings27,28,29, our system operates far outside the Josephson regime. The Josephson effect requires the junction length to be much shorter than the superconducting coherence length, which for our system is close to the healing length4,12. In our case, the channel length ℓ = 27 μm is much larger than the estimated healing length ξ ≈ 1.2 μm (Methods, ‘Estimate of ξ’). Moreover, we observe neither a well-defined current-phase relation nor an oscillation amplitude consistent with the Josephson relation. The former statement is based on time-of-flight measurements of the relative phase of the two reservoirs with the same preparation performed in a slightly different geometry. Although for the data shown in this manuscript, we always observe the same initial dynamics (up to small noise), these additional measurements confirm that the prepared phase between the two reservoirs is not controlled, sampling values between 0 and 2π from a flat distribution. We therefore conclude that the oscillatory signal observed in our experiment cannot be attributed to JO.

According to recent reports, extended Data Fig. 2 provides additional data related to Fig. 3. The theoretical motivation and the \({\chi }_{\nu }^{2}\) analysis presented in Fig. 2 already justify the choice of models. The data shown here complements that analysis by demonstrating that the scaling laws reported in Fig. 3 are not numerical artefacts and are not imposed by the fitting procedure.

It has been revealed that for both the LAMH and vortex models, the predicted scalings break down outside their respective ranges of validity. This behaviour indicates that the observed scaling is not a numerical consequence of the fitting procedure and is not artificially enforced by the functional form of the models.

The saturation of the LAMH-inferred resistance at large widths does not seem to be due to limited fitting precision, fitting boundaries or lack of convergence. Instead, it reflects a transition from the strong exponential width dependence characteristic of the LAMH model to a much weaker dependence, as predicted by the vortex model.

For the vortex model, the trend reverses in the crossover regime, showing a clear deviation from the scaling expected by that model.

Kai Havertz has become Arteta’s preferred striker, leaving Gyökeres fighting for opportunities despite showing signs of improvement in recent weeks.

There is a strong argument that Arsenal can upgrade at centre-forward, but selling Gyökeres too quickly would be risky.

In a recent development, that feels like the correct approach. Gyökeres may not be Arteta’s ideal striker, but he still provides power, movement in behind and a completely different option to Havertz. Arsenal are competing across several competitions, and one injury could rapidly make his role much more crucial.

Álvarez would undoubtedly represent an upgrade in terms of pressing, combination play and tactical versatility, but signing him would be extremely expensive and far from straightforward.

Arsenal should therefore avoid forcing Gyökeres out simply because another striker is preferred.

According to recent reports, if Álvarez or another elite No.9 becomes realistically available, then a summer change could make sense. Until that happens, Gyökeres remains valuable depth rather than a problem that urgently needs solving.

From this coming weekend onwards, following a short but gruelling trip to Anfield to face rivals Liverpool, United players will no longer be allowed days off immediately after matches, with the exception of those returning from lengthy European away trips.

Meanwhile, the third and final measure will see the introduction of a pre-match squad meal, designed to keep tabs on players' nutrition while also bringing the group closer together.

The Red Devils are rapidly back in action midweek against Sporting CP, as they look to secure their third win of the 2026–27 Champions League league phase.   • The Financial Times first reported on Huang's affair with Alice H., an executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based customer of Nvidia, which has been suspected of trying to circumvent export controls to get advanced Nvidia chips into China.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang's admission to an affair with a woman whom US intelligence officials believe was working as a spy for China could have profound implications for the $5 trillion (€4.47 trillion) company.

The Financial Times first reported on Huang's affair with Alice H., an executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based customer of Nvidia, which has been suspected of trying to circumvent export controls to get advanced Nvidia chips into China.

The newspaper reported that the US government and its intelligence community believe she was recruited as a spy by China's Ministry of State Security intelligence agency.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

US government officials drafted a memo about the allegations shortly before US President Donald Trump traveled to Beijing for a summit with Xi Jinping in May.

Huang's relationship with the alleged Chinese spy has exposed him and the company to criticism that it may have allowed China to obtain valuable trade secrets as Beijing tries to gain an edge in the race to develop advanced AI models.

Sources indicate that nvidia is initiating an investigation led by independent board members and an external law firm. It said in a statement that Huang "has been the target of a foreign intelligence effort.".

Industry observers note that "The board prioritizes US national and economic security, which is paramount to the interests of Nvidia and its shareholders," the company noted Sunday. "While the board has no reason to believe that either national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised, the board's inquiry will examine all available information.".

The tech giant's shares fell in early trading on Monday.

While US intelligence officials have not commented publicly on the claims, Trump — with whom Jensen Huang has a close relationship — has backed the Nvidia boss.

Industry observers note that "He's an honorable guy," mentioned Trump. "I have not spoken to him ​about it. I just know he's a ​fine person, but you never know what is going on. I hope everything's fine.".

Tim Culpan, an Asia tech reporter who has covered Nvidia and Huang closely for years, told DW that while Nvidia's fundamental strengths as a company remain in place, Huang is hugely personally damaged by the story.

"They're still going to make great chips and they're going to sell them to millions of customers around the world who want the best AI chips in the world," he mentioned.

"His opinion is going to carry a lot less weight now. And that, in the long term, will flow through to Nvidia and Nvidia's own corporate interests. So it won't be immediate. It's really a fact that he doesn't have the sway or the power that he might have had one week ago simply through this.".

Richard Windsor, a tech analyst and the founder of research tech giant Radio Free Mobile, mentioned the news could be very serious for Nvidia given how much the company has revolved around Huang for decades.

"This problem is particularly acute because Jensen Huang is very hands-on, meaning that the key decisions that led to its success were ultimately taken by him and because there is no obvious successor," he said.

"I suspect we are about to find out just how much the market thinks that the manufacturer is dependent on its iconic founder and CEO.".

Nvidia and Huang's attitude toward China and potential Chinese customers has been a bone of contention with US intelligence officials — despite Huang's close relationship with Trump.

Huang has repeatedly lobbied Trump to ease restrictions on the sale of Nvidia chips to China. A 2025 export control deal heavily curbed sales, but Trump subsequently permitted the export of older H200 Nvidia chips to China in return for the US government receiving a cut of the sales.

Sources indicate that however, that deal has been complicated and bogged down by Washington's strict export-license review. China has also initiated import controls, despite strong demand from Chinese companies. China lacks access to the most advanced AI-capable chips. Beijing wants to develop its own alternatives but has struggled to catch up.

Huang has argued that Chinese dependence on Nvidia's chips would prevent rivals such as Huawei from catching up and boosting China's ambitions to dominate AI supply chains.

It has been revealed that however, that argument has been dismissed by many US intelligence officials. They fear that unlimited Chinese access to the most advanced Nvidia chips would boost China's domestic AI sector, lead to its AI models catching up with the leading US models and see the chips being used in Chinese military applications.

The US-China rivalry has become a central theme in the global AI story, with both countries seeking to gain an upper hand in the technology. Leading US AI executives such as Anthropic's Dario Amodei have argued that US AI companies can't afford to take a prolonged pause to allow safety standards in AI to catch up, if they're going to prevent Chinese firms from gaining an advantage.

Washington's central fear over Huang's affair is that it could have led to Beijing obtaining vital trade secrets or other key information about how Nvidia makes its most advanced chips.

Windsor thinks Huang will survive the "severe test" due to his importance to the company. He also cast doubt on the extent to which Beijing and its leading tech firms have learned from Nvidia's chips, pointing to China's own chip ambitions and commitment to have its firms buy its own semiconductors.

"I am far from convinced that Chinese AI has materially benefited from technology or illicit chip imports that it gained from Nvidia," he noted.

The news comes at a particularly challenging moment for Nvidia, which has benefited massively from the AI boom thanks to its position as the leading maker of cutting-edge semiconductors needed for AI applications.

Nvidia's valuation has soared dramatically in recent years as companies rushed to buy its chips, becoming the world's first $5 trillion firm in October 2025.

In a recent development, however, doubts over the sustainability of the $9 trillion capital expenditure AI boom have sparked a major sell-off in stocks related to the boom in recent weeks. The Democrats' sweeping victories in the US midterms have added to the doubts, given the strength of voter opposition to data center construction in the US.

In a recent development, manchester United and Liverpool form one of the defining rivalries in the history of English football. The nation's two most successful clubs have battled against one another armed with some of the finest players the game has ever seen.

The highest scorers in this derby between northern giants include England captains, Premier League legends and Ballon d'Or winners. But there are some notable absentees. Liverpool's all-time top scorer, Ian Rush, only netted three of his 346 goals against the Red Devils, while Manchester United icon Sir Bobby Charlton mustered just four.

Liverpool's modern-day legend Mohamed Salah scarcely suffered from stage fright during this grand fixture, seemingly extending his record goal haul with every encounter against United. Here are the other players who did deliver.

All-Time Top Scorers in Man Utd vs Liverpool.

Sources indicate that individual insults are a sign of respect in the fickle world of football fandom. During a 3-0 humbling at Anfield in April 1964, United's lithe forward Denis Law was targeted by the boisterous home fans who broke into a spontaneous rendition of "Eee, Aye, Addio, Denis Law's a twerp".

Sources indicate that law would only have to wait a year for his revenge, scoring twice in a 3-0 victory over Liverpool at Old Trafford. The fleet-footed Scot was a man possessed, thumping a volley beyond Tommy Lawrence before following the ball over the line and into the net in the second half. Law got a nasty gash on his knee for his troubles, but the stitches would have been softened by the sweet taste of victory against United's biggest rivals.

Only Salah has scored more goals than Robbie Fowler in the Premier League era for Liverpool. Fowler rattled in 128, putting him ahead of the likes of Steven Gerrard, Michael Owen and Sadio Mane. Six of that hulking haul came against Man United.

The Liverpool academy graduate soon became known as 'God', thanks in no small part to his devastating derby displays in the 1995/96 campaign. Fowler bagged back-to-back braces against United that season, helping his boyhood club take four points off the eventual Premier League champions. Fowler also enjoyed success against the Red Devils while he was at Manchester City, scoring three times.

The entire English top flight was interested in Bryan Robson after he emerged as one of the nation's most talented players at West Bromwich Albion. Man United beat Liverpool in the race for the midfielder's signature in 1981 and the Merseyside outfit would repeatedly suffer at the hands of their former target.

Robson scored both goals in a Charity Shield victory over Liverpool to begin the 1983/84 campaign, at a time when the contest was viewed as a friendly match. Robson ensured he left his mark in the high-stakes setting of an FA Cup semi-final against Liverpool - not once, but twice.

Sources indicate that united's buccaneering captain opened the scoring in a dramatic 2-2 draw at Goodison Park before finding the net again in the replay four days later. United advanced to the Wembley final, where Robson hoisted the FA Cup trophy in triumph.

In a recent development, for an all too brief period, no team on the continent could stop Man United's George Best. Liverpool were no different. Between 1965 and 1968, Best scored seven goals in as many appearances against the Reds.

If you'd given me the choice of going out and beating four men and smashing a goal in from 30 yards against Liverpool or going to bed with Miss World, it would have been a difficult choice. Luckily, I had both.

A spell-binding blend of flair and ruthless finishing, Best scored both goals in a rare Anfield defeat for Liverpool in 1967 at the tender age of 21.

The Northern Ireland international may have been one of Man United's greatest academy products, but he got his nickname from a Merseyside institution. The so-called 'Fifth Beatle' sported the same shaggy haircut as the Liverpool-based group and attracted just as much attention from fans scattered across the country.

Manchester United must have been sick of the sight of Liverpool's Harry Chambers by the end of the 1920/21 campaign. The bow-legged striker scored in four different games against the Red Devils that season. Only two other players in the club's history - Rush and Salah - have ever achieved such a feat for the Reds, but never against their fiercest rivals.

The First World War delayed his professional debut, but Chambers made up for lost time when United came to town. One of Liverpool's all-time top scorers was adored by Anfield for his unflinchingly joyful demeanour, earning the nickname 'Smiler'. A lethal record against United didn't harm his popularity either.

Since making his first-team debut for the club back in 2015, Marcus Rashford has made over 400 appearances for his boyhood club. He has won five major trophies, including the 2024 FA Cup, which saw them beat Man City in the final after Rashford netted in a thrilling 4-3 quarter-final victory over Liverpool.

Recent findings suggest that the England international's best performance against the Merseyside club came back in March 2018, when he scored a brace in a 2-1 win. The first of his two goals that day was a trademark finish for the winger as he cut back onto his right foot on the edge of the box before curling the ball into the bottom corner.

For the Salford-born inside forward, simply playing for his boyhood club was the stuff of dreams. Stan Pearson advanced beyond the realm of fantasy with a hat-trick against Liverpool shortly after the resumption of professional football following the Second World War. No United player scored another treble against the Reds until Dimitar Berbatov's hat-trick 64 years later.

Pearson was more commonly lauded for his ability to create goals rather than score them, yet unlocked a prolific edge in meetings with Liverpool.

Location was not a consideration for the forward, who plundered goals at the same reliable rate as United embarked upon a nomadic stretch after Old Trafford was bombed during the Second World War. It wasn't until 1953, when he scored his eighth and final goal against Liverpool, that Pearson found the net in this fixture at United's traditional home.

It has been revealed that the hard-nosed Dick Forshaw is the only Liverpool player to ever score two hat-tricks against Man United. His pair of trebles both came at Anfield within 12 months of each other in the mid-1920s.

Forshaw delivered a blunt reminder of top-flight football's ruthlessness on United's first trip to Merseyside since promotion in 1925. Those who braved the miserable conditions that day demanded more goals after Forshaw completed his hat-trick in a 5-0 thrashing. Liverpool's robust number nine helped himself to another treble in a more even 4-2 victory the following year.

It has been revealed that in between his Anfield heroics, Forshaw scored again against United at Old Trafford in March 1926, prompting strong calls from the press for his international debut. Forshaw never earned an England cap and left Liverpool under a cloud by agreeing to join Merseyside rivals Everton. At least he didn't move to Manchester.

Steven Gerrard was taught the importance of his boyhood club's rivalry with Man United from a young age. The rampaging midfielder from a devout Liverpool family was a fan of Bryan Robson and tried on his friend's number seven United shirt one afternoon. Gerrard's father was not impressed.

Industry observers note that honest to God, I thought I was going to have to move house! I was only a baby but I was convinced Dad would kick me out for putting on that United shirt.

Based on the insatiable hunger that Gerrard took into every encounter with United, he never forgot that childhood lesson.

The rivalry could get the better of Gerrard at times - most notably in his final encounter with United, when he was sent off 38 seconds after coming on as a half-time substitute. But more often than not, Liverpool's passionate skipper staked his claim to be one of the club's greatest players of all time in these derbies.

An integral figure in Man United's first top-flight title secured during the 1907/08 campaign, George Wall found the net in both fixtures against Liverpool that season. Wall scored United's second in a 4-0 thrashing that September but was limited to a pair of consolation efforts as the league leaders slumped to a 7-4 humbling at Anfield six months later.

Three days after the derby dismantling, Wall got United back on track with two goals in a 4-1 victory over Sheffield Wednesday. The speedy left-winger never replicated his scoring exploits of that triumphant campaign, but he was reliable against the Reds, finding the net six more times before the outbreak of the First World War.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Two football images adorn the walls of Martin Tyler’s new home or at least they will when everything is in order.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By MATT BARLOW, FOOTBALL WRITER.

Published: 13:55 EST, 18 November 2026 | Updated: 15:04 EST, 18 November 2026.

Two football images adorn the walls of Martin Tyler’s new home or at least they will when everything is in order.

Tyler has recently moved house and the large, framed photograph of Teddy Sheringham scoring for Nottingham Forest against Liverpool, the only goal of the first Premier League game broadcast live by Sky is still on the floor by the front door.

From wherever it ends up, it will project a moment in time when everything changed for Tyler, having walked away from a steady job at ITV and taken a leap of faith as lead commentator for the new satellite channel.

'A new frontier,' admits Tyler, the undisputed ‘Voice of the Premier League’ by the time he left the role at Sky, more than 30 years later.

'We didn’t know where it would take us, so that was a special day. Feeling a bit like a pioneer. Wondering whether we were all on a fool’s errand. Some people turned down the job I accepted because of the risk. My kids were four and two at the time.

'We used to travel to the games by train in those days, and we would look out of the window and count the satellite dishes as we passed through a significant town. We didn’t know whether it was going to work. I wasn’t sure anybody would be watching.

Legendary football commentator Martin Tyler has released a book: TALES FROM THE GANTRY.

Tyler was the undoubted 'Voice of the Premier League' by the time he left Sky Sports in 2023.

'It was slow off the ground and there was a feeling within the game against live football, that people wouldn’t go to the games if they were televised live, and it ended up the opposite. Attendances have gone up, an amazing paradox. Now you can’t get a ticket.'.

Televised football has come a long way since Tyler’s first commentary game, Southampton v Sheffield Wednesday in the old Division Two in 1974, shot with just four cameras for Southern Television.

Recent findings suggest that 'Now if you don’t have 24 cameras you can feel a bit short-changed,' he laughs. 'I worked at ITV for about 17 years, most of it commentating and you would get a crew on match day who had been doing Coronation Street or Emmerdale Farm in the week and a match director from light entertainment.'.

It has been revealed that the Premier League has come a long way, too. Some might argue too far. It has led football from its roots as the working man’s game to a place where clubs are owned by nations states and mired in the legal complications of the Manchester City case.

Tyler wants to reserve comment on City’s financial offences until sentencing is passed, aware he is inextricably bound to their success because of his iconic commentary for Sergio Aguero’s winner in the 93rd minute against Queen’s Park Rangers to snatch the Premier League title from Manchester United in 2012.

'I’ve always noted you won’t see anything like it again, and I stick to that,' he says, although he the 'Aguero moment’ as it has become commonly known probably means less to him than it does to others.

He is proud to deliver the words but insists those moments belong to the players, the clubs and the fans, not to him.

Ask about his favourite game from three decades in the Premier League and Tyler instinctively pulls Liverpool’s 4-3 comeback win against Newcastle in 1996 from the thrillers he has called.

His own footballing background, meanwhile, could hardly be any further from the Premier League’s glitzy, moneyed elite.

It has been revealed that tyler has always supported Woking and played as an amateur for Corinthian-Casuals. 'The law was you couldn’t get paid,' he indicates. 'We were on expenses only and they weren’t dodgy expenses. If I went on the tube to Leytonstone, I got the tube fare repaid and no more.

According to recent reports, 'I played for five years at that level and never got a penny because that was the rule. I played my last game in 1973 and within two years’ they got rid of it because so many people were bending the rules. An opposition player told me their team were on £75 a game.'.

Tyler reflected on his time in the game as a player, coach and commentator with Daily Mail Sport's Matt Barlow.

He was famously on commentary for Sergio Aguero's title-winning moment in 2012.

From a cricketing family, Tyler was on the books at Surrey where he twice served as 12th man and lived for a time with Bob Willis, who became one of England’s greatest fast bowlers after moving on to Warwickshire.

In a recent development, his manager for a time at Casuals was Surrey legend Micky Stewart, who had also played for the famous amateur football club before turning professional at Charlton. In those days it was possible for the multi-talented to hold down a decent career in two sports.

An afternoon in Tyler’s company is just as likely to involve digressions into non-league football, where he worked as an assistant to Alan Dowson at clubs including Woking and Hampton & Richmond, as it is into the Premier League.

He might regale you with a story about Arsene Wenger and the time, on the way to the gantry at Wigan Athletic, he slipped deeper than he realised into long conversation with the then Arsenal boss about rioting in Paris and almost missed his pre-match slot.

And he might pivot from there into Wenger’s fierce rivalry with Sir Alex Ferguson. 'I have seen Arsene very, very grumpy,' claims Tyler. 'When he lost the FA Cup semi-final when Dennis Bergkamp missed the penalty and Ryan Giggs scored.

In a recent development, 'I have never seen a manager so angry because he knew he had handed over not only an FA Cup final place but also the domination they enjoyed at that time. They had done the Double in 98 and he felt that was not only about losing a match but losing their psychological edge over their greatest rivals. He was livid. Talk about winning and losing with dignity.'.

But there’s every chance he will reminisce about the time when, as a schoolboy Woking supporter in the terrible winter of 1962-63 he was rewarded for volunteering to paint the stands with an invitation to travel on the team bus to an Amateur Cup tie at Lydbrook Athletic.

Industry observers note that 'We left Woking at seven on the morning of the match for a two o’clock kick-off in Gloucestershire and by nine we were digging the bus out of a snowdrift on the A4,' says Tyler. 'We got there at four, no floodlights, and they had marked the lines on the snow with blue soap powder but there was no way we could play. We turned around to go back, got stuck in Cheltenham and had to stay for the night.'.

The only other footballing image on display in Tyler’s home is a photograph of him and Dowson celebrating as the final whistle confirmed their Hampton & Richmond side as Isthmian League champions in 2016.

Tyler has had a hugely varied career, all the way from grassroots level right to the top.

Tyler even worked as an assistant coach to Alan Dowson at several Non-League clubs.

TALES FROM THE GANTRY: Letters from a Lifetime in Football by Martin Tyler is published by Pitch and out now HERE.

After collecting the trophy, Tyler jumped into his car, drove north and less than 24 hours later was at the King Power Stadium to see Leicester crowned champions of England.

Industry observers note that 'The greatest fairytale story in the Premier League,' as he states. 'I had sampled that in a tiny non-league way, then taken those feelings with me to Leicester where it was multiplied a million times, but I could tell the world a tiny bit about how wonderful they must be feeling.'.

Industry observers note that the range of his experience is vast. From amateur football in the 60s, through regional television and ITV to Sky’s Premier League revolution. He commentates regularly and coaches at Woking’s academy and has written a book.

Sources indicate that it is a wonderful compilation of 110 essays, the reflections on his lifetime in football. 'The random thoughts of a football obsessive,' as he likes to call it.

TALES FROM THE GANTRY: Letters from a Lifetime in Football by Martin Tyler is published by Pitch and out now HERE.

In a recent development, it is an all-Premier League tie at Anfield as Liverpool host Chelsea in the last 16 of the League Cup, with a place in the quarter-finals at stake. This will be the first managerial meeting between childhood friends Andoni Iraola and Xabi Alonso.

According to recent reports, liverpool beat Tottenham 3-1 at Anfield in the last round of this competition, which included a stunning goal from Dominik Szoboszlai to seal progression to the last 16. They earned their first home Premier League win of the season on the weekend as they beat Brighton 2-0. Iraola’s men come into this game off the back of four straight wins in all competitions.

According to recent reports, “There will definitely be changes, but we want to win the game and we want to be competitive,” Iraola noted ahead of this tie. “We have to see how the legs; we are not just in the Carabao Cup, but also in the Champions League and we have been trying to make changes from game to game. We want to be in the next round. We have been unlucky in the draw, playing Chelsea, and they have been unlucky also. But we want to be in the draw again and that only happens if you win. We need to rotate, all the top teams need to rotate when you are playing every three days. Sometimes you are forced to rotate due to injury or sometimes different demands in different games tactically. I am happy that everyone is involved. When we have had to use someone who has not played a lot of games, they have helped us. The more players we have in a good place, the easier my selection will be, even if it is hard to leave players out.”.

Giovanni Leoni, Conor Bradley and Hugo Ekitike remain long-term absentees for the hosts with Jeremie Frimpong also missing. Florian Wirtz could feature despite going off with an ankle knock during the win over Brighton.

Like Liverpool, Chelsea also had an all-Premier League tie in the third round of this competition, beating Leeds 6-3 in a high-scoring affair at Stamford Bridge. Chelsea come into tonight’s game off the back of a 2-0 defeat against Tottenham in the league last weekend. Not only did they lose on Saturday but to make matters worse for them Cole Palmer was sent off. As a result of that red card, Palmer is suspended for tonight’s tie.

“We [Alonso and Palmer] spoke and for sure he knows the mistake he made,” Alonso remarked. “Things that you can avoid. I hope that this is not going to be repeated. He is aware of that, he is mature and it was a mistake. He is in a good space, he connects very well socially with his teammates. They like him, they want Cole smiling, they want Cole having fun, enjoying his game because when we see that, he will have a better team. I will just ask you because he has got this very cool persona, you probably know his personality is very interesting.”.

In a recent development, former Liverpool midfielder and current Chelsea boss Alonso has lost his two games as a manager against Liverpool; a 4-0 defeat as Bayer Leverkusen boss and then a 1-0 loss when in charge of Real Madrid, with both taking place at Anfield. Alonso is not the only ex-Liverpool midfielder to return to Anfield tonight as their former captain Jordan Henderson is in the Chelsea squad for tonight. Joao Pedro has missed the trip to Anfield because of a thigh injury which could rule him out for a few weeks.

The Premier league fixture between these sides at Anfield ended in a 1-1 draw back in May. In that match, Arne Slot was in charge of Liverpool with Calum McFarlane in interim charge of Chelsea. Chelsea won the reverse fixture 2-1 at Stamford Bridge. Team news from Anfield to follow shortly.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Arsenal’s long-running interest in Vinícius Júnior refuses to disappear, with Real Madrid reportedly placing a minimum €150million valuation on the Brazilian should his future change next summer.

Mikel Arteta’s side pushed hard to sign Vinícius before he eventually committed his future to Madrid, and fresh speculation suggests the Gunners are still watching his situation closely.

However, any deal would require one of the biggest financial commitments in Arsenal’s history.

According to Josep Pedrerol, speaking on El Chiringuito and quoted in his latest update, Real Madrid would not consider selling Vinícius for anything below €150million.

Crucially, Madrid have not actively placed the winger on the market. Pedrerol has since clarified that Vinícius presently wants to stay and Real Madrid want to keep him, meaning the valuation only becomes relevant if the 26-year-old asks to leave.

Arsenal nevertheless remain interested after pursuing him aggressively during the summer.

Recent findings suggest that that pursuit was more serious than simple speculation. CaughtOffside reports that Arsenal remain confident they could eventually convince Vinícius to move to the Emirates, despite his latest Real Madrid contract running until 2032.

There is little doubt about the footballing appeal.

Industry observers note that arsenal have been searching for an elite left-sided attacker capable of providing the same game-changing threat Bukayo Saka offers from the opposite flank. Vinícius would solve that problem instantly.

His pace, one-versus-one ability and experience delivering in the Champions League would take Arsenal’s attack to another level.

But €150m changes the conversation completely.

A transfer at that price would smash Arsenal’s record and could force Andrea Berta to create significant room in both the wage bill and squad before a deal becomes realistic.

There is also no guarantee Vinícius will actually want to leave Madrid. For that reason, Arsenal should stay patient rather than structure their entire recruitment strategy around one superstar.

Sources indicate that if Vinícius becomes genuinely available, Arsenal are now substantial enough and ambitious enough to enter the conversation. But paying €150m only makes sense if Arteta believes he is the final piece capable of turning an already elite side into Europe’s dominant team.

It has been revealed that monza star Varela has already attracted interest from several clubs around Europe. The latest report from Corriere dello Sport claims that Premier League sides Tottenham, Brentford and Sunderland have already sounded out the striker’s availability, while Liverpool regularly send scouts to watch him.

Varela is a fresh Monza signing, joining the newly promoted Serie A side over the summer on a €2.5m deal from Benfica.

The 21-year-old has scored nine goals in ten Serie A games so far this season, resulting in the best scorer in Italy’s top flight.

Other European clubs, including Juventus, Napoli and Arsenal, have recently been linked with a January move for the Portuguese striker, who has recently received his first senior call-up with his national team.

His former club Benfica do not have an option to re-sign him, but only retain a 20% sell-on clause and can match any offer Monza receive in the coming years.

According to multilpe sources, Monza’s asking price for Varela is €40m.
