Data are presented as mean ± s.d., with the individual value for each replicate overlaid as a dot; n = 3 replicate cultures per group, split from a single primary PDAC CAF isolate and treated and sequenced independently. Statistical significance was assessed using two-sided unpaired Student’s t-tests (equal variances assumed), and exact P values are displayed above the corresponding comparison bars.

The CellChat and NicheNet findings that ISG15+ iCAFs were putatively IFNγ responsive led us to further explore whether IFNγ stimulation could polarize fibroblasts towards the ISG15+ iCAF state. On the basis of the previous work, we also hypothesized that fibroblasts could be activated towards the CXCL8+ iCAF state in response to lipopolysaccharide (LPS) or IL-1 exposure66. To test these hypotheses, we treated cultured human primary pancreatic CAFs with IFNγ, LPS or vehicle control for 24 h, followed by bulk RNA-seq (Fig. 4c,d and Supplementary Fig. 16a). Both treatments successfully upregulated their respective canonical response pathways (Fig. 4e,f, Supplementary Table 10 and Supplementary Fig. 16b,c). Direct gene signature comparisons revealed that the ISG15+ and CXCL8+ iCAF transcriptional profiles were maximally enriched in the IFNγ-treated and LPS-treated cohorts, respectively (Fig. 4g,h). Although this transcriptional concordance is compelling, in vivo CAF phenotypes are undoubtedly shaped by complex, multifactorial microenvironmental cues. Nevertheless, these experiments support the biological relevance of our identified iCAF signatures.

Industry observers note that to evaluate the cross-species conservation of these cell subpopulations, we expanded our atlas to include mouse models, the primary experimental system for solid tumour research67. Applying our established analytical framework, we evaluated more than 2.5 million cells across 526 samples from 68 mouse solid tumour datasets (Fig. 1a,b and Supplementary Table 1). To manage the computational scale, individual datasets underwent an identical sketching, three-way integration and full-dataset projection pipeline detailed previously (Extended Data Fig. 8a–c). This parallel approach successfully delineated the same seven major cell lineages observed in the human TME (Extended Data Figs. 8d–f and 9a and Supplementary Table 11), which were highly conserved across nearly all mouse cancer types (Extended Data Fig. 9b,c).

Applying our recursive integration and reclustering pipeline to the mouse stromal compartment, we evaluated the heterogeneity of fibroblast, endothelial, mural and nerve populations (Supplementary Table 12). Mouse CAFs segregated into four broad subpopulations corresponding to the human TME: apCAFs, iCAFs, mCAFs and ssCAFs (Extended Data Figs. 9d and 10a and Supplementary Fig. 17). Crucially, the Isg15+ iCAF state, which our human data suggest as a direct responder to chronic IFNγ from tumour-reactive TEX cells, was highly conserved in mice. By contrast, because mice lack a direct CXCL8 orthologue, the second human iCAF state (CXCL8+) aligned with a functionally analogous Spp1+ iCAF population in mice. Furthermore, we did not observe a clear mouse equivalent to the human COL4A1+LRRC15− mCAF population. Both mouse ssCAF subpopulations were broadly conserved; however, the transcriptional equivalent of the human CXCL14+ state was defined primarily by Cxcl12 expression in mice. Of note, mouse apCAFs expressed mesothelial markers such as Msln42, suggesting a potential distinct lineage origin compared with their human counterparts (Extended Data Fig. 10a and Supplementary Fig. 17).

Within the endothelial compartment, we identified subpopulations matching the human TME: artery, capillary, lymphatic, vein and, importantly, Esm1+ tip cells (Extended Data Figs. 9e and 10b and Supplementary Fig. 18). The conservation of these Esm1+ tip cells across nearly all mouse tumour types (Extended Data Fig. 9e′) provides a robust cross-species model for studying the myeloid-driven angiogenic axis identified in our human atlas. Mural cells constituted a smaller fraction of the mouse TME (0.46%) than humans (1.3%), consistent with limited recruitment pools in many mouse hosts68. Nevertheless, we identified conserved mural subpopulations: Ccl2+ pericytes, Cd248+ pericytes and an umbrella group of smooth muscle cells (Extended Data Figs. 9f,f′ and 10c and Supplementary Fig. 19). Finally, as in humans, both myelinating (Mpz+) and non-myelinating (Ngfr+) Schwann cells were present (Extended Data Figs. 9g,g′ and 10d and Supplementary Fig. 20); however, mouse melanocytes were not readily distinguishable in our analysis.

Overall, these tumour stromal subpopulations appear largely conserved across mouse cancer types, and their relative abundances in tumour compared with non-malignant samples mirror those of the analogous human subpopulations (Fig. 3a, Supplementary Table 13 and Supplementary Fig. 21). Isg15+ iCAFs, Esm1+ tip endothelial cells and Cd248+ pericytes were consistently enriched in malignant tissues across both species, reinforcing their conserved roles as foundational components of TME dysfunction.

Sources indicate that consistent with our human datasets, immune cells constituted the largest component of the mouse TME, with over 749,000 cells recursively isolated into broad lymphoid and myeloid lineages (Extended Data Fig. 1g–j). Among lymphoid cells, we identified seven T cell, two B cell, one natural killer cell and one plasma cell populations, all closely mirroring those identified in humans (Extended Data Fig. 9h,h′ and Supplementary Fig. 22). Crucially, this included a conserved population of exhausted T cells (Pdcd1+ TEX), confirming the presence of the putative upstream signalling drivers of the Isg15+ iCAF inflammatory axis within the mouse atlas. Similarly, mouse myeloid analysis delineated 14 putative subpopulations, composed primarily of dendritic cells, monocytes and macrophages—the conserved source of the myeloid-driven angiogenic signalling to Esm1+ tip cells—alongside mast cells, neutrophils and osteoclasts (Extended Data Fig. 9i,i′ and Supplementary Fig. 23). Overall, these findings underscore the deep transcriptional concordance between the human and mouse immune microenvironments.

Finally, we assessed the evolutionary conservation of stromal and immune cells between human and mouse tumours. For fibroblasts, we first pooled all 554,238 CAFs isolated from both species and performed orthologue transformation of the mouse data into a shared human gene space. Cells within the resultant datasets were integrated on a per-study basis using Harmony (Fig. 5a, left), demonstrating that CAF subpopulations were largely conserved (Fig. 5a, right). Specifically, the iCAF, mCAF and ssCAF populations overlapped strongly within the integrated uniform manifold approximation and projection (UMAP) embedding, whereas apCAF populations exhibited moderate discordance, possibly reflecting distinct lineage origins tied to Msln expression.

Industry observers note that a, Human and mouse CAF atlases were merged and re-integrated using Harmony (left), showing substantial overlap between the human and mouse fibroblast subpopulations (middle). Spearman correlations were calculated based on co-incidence among underlying clusters (right). n = 554,238 cells. b–f, Merged and re-integrated human and mouse tumour atlases for endothelial (b; n = 296,957), mural (c; n = 173,859), nerve (d; n = 10,129), lymphoid (e; n = 1,913,684) and myeloid (f; n = 1,221,301) cells using Harmony, with correlation matrices derived as described for panel a.

We similarly performed integrative cross-species analyses on the endothelial (296,957 cells), mural (173,859 cells) and nerve (10,129 cells) compartments (Fig. 5b–d, left). Endothelial and mural subpopulations proved highly conserved across species (Fig. 5b,c, right). By contrast, within the nerve compartment, only a minor population of Schwann cells exhibited interspecies overlap (Fig. 5d, right). Furthermore, integration of the massive immune TME (1,913,684 lymphoid and 1,221,301 myeloid cells; Fig. 5e,f, left) revealed robust evolutionary conservation of subpopulations across both broad lineages (Fig. 5e,f, right).

In a recent development, to formally quantify this conservation, we evaluated the shared overlap of populations across co-clustering integrations, generating heatmaps as proxies for cellular transcriptomic alignment (Fig. 5a–f, right). An orthogonal analysis utilizing anchor-based label transfer of annotated mouse datasets projected onto their human counterparts yielded parallel results (Supplementary Fig. 24a–f). Both quantitative assessments revealed striking cross-species correlations for all non-nerve subpopulations. In summary, this cross-species integration demonstrates that the core transcriptomic states defining the TME are highly conserved between human and mouse solid tumours.

Here we have presented a formal meta-analysis of more than 15 million cells across 42 types of solid tumours in humans and mice, providing unprecedented insight into the highly conserved cellular ecosystem of the TME. By leveraging parallel, semi-orthogonal integration strategies, we established a highly robust, inclusive framework for resolving distinct cluster-wise annotations across massive, heterogeneous datasets. Through this approach, we selectively isolated distinct cell subpopulations within the shared stromal and immune compartments, enabling a pan-cancer mapping of the TME that also captures transitional and peripheral cell states often lost in standard single-pipeline approaches.

Recent findings suggest that by harmonizing our atlas-level clusters with established paradigms13,25,38,39,40,41, we developed a unified framework that resolves the overlapping stromal descriptions in the literature. For fibroblasts, we delineated four overarching superclusters: apCAFs, iCAFs, mCAFs and ssCAFs, as well as multiple subclusters. The massive scale of this atlas allowed us to consolidate previously fragmented nomenclature. For instance, we grouped both classical LRRC15+ myofibroblastic and COL4A1/SPP1+ mechanoresponsive states into a unified mCAF compartment, reflecting their shared ECM-remodelling programming. Furthermore, our orthogonal analyses consistently indicate that the traditional CXCL12+ iCAF state would be better defined as a tissue-resident ssCAF population (CXCL14/CXCL12+), transcriptionally distinct from true inflammatory iCAFs. For endothelial, mural and nerve cells, we have similarly provided nomenclature that clarifies previous descriptions in smaller studies8,52.

A consequence of these refined classifications is the emergence of more precisely specialized cellular states. For example, within the iCAF compartment, we resolved a distinct subpopulation defined by ISG15 expression. These cells are strongly enriched in tumours and across stages of neoplastic growth, exhibit gene expression patterns consistent with receiving IFNγ signalling from T cells and correlate with significantly decreased survival. This suggests that these ISG15+ iCAFs represent an important component of the immunosuppressive TME and a promising therapeutic target.

In a recent development, the identification of ISG15+ iCAFs underscores a primary clinical implication of this atlas: the profound conservation of the stroma suggests that targeting such core populations could yield broadly applicable multicancer therapeutics. By systematically isolating fibroblast, endothelial and mural populations that are distinctly tumour enriched and linked to poor clinical outcomes, this framework transitions from a descriptive atlas to a therapeutic blueprint, offering the potential to selectively modulate pro-tumorigenic stroma while avoiding the off-target toxicity frequently associated with traditional interventions.

Consistent with our findings in the stroma, we observed an equally high degree of conservation within the immune microenvironment of solid tumours, providing a parallel, broadly applicable framework for lymphoid and myeloid populations. Although combinatorial immunotherapies are rapidly being adopted, their efficacy fundamentally hinges on the permissiveness of the TME. Yet, these immune populations are rarely analysed in the context of broader stromal diversity. By establishing a consistent cellular framework across both compartments, we have provided a unified lens to evaluate antitumour immunity within the TME as a whole. As a proof of principle, we have provided supporting evidence for selected immune–stromal interactions predicted by our meta-analysis by eliciting the expected transcriptional shifts within treated stromal cells.

In a recent development, overall, this study is considerably larger in scope than previous seminal studies in the field. This study also assessed all cells within the TME, whereas most previous work has either examined only single-cell types in isolation or been limited to either the tumour stromal or immune compartments. By establishing the high degree of cross-species conservation between human and mouse TMEs, this atlas bridges a critical gap in translating preclinical models to human disease. We complemented our computational framework with in vitro and in vivo assays to link predicted cellular states with observable tumour biology. Moreover, by codifying these findings into a public toolkit, we have provided a standardized reference framework that enables automated label transfer and reference mapping to assist in analysing new cancer datasets.

This meta-analysis provides a foundational resource for interpreting the cellular diversity of the stromal and immune components of solid tumours. To ensure broad accessibility, we have released an interactive web portal for independent dataset exploration (tmeatlas.stanford.edu) alongside an R package (scTME) designed to systematically project and annotate these classifications onto external datasets. Moreover, the underlying code, including the central pipeline for atlas construction and custom scripts for downstream analysis, is publicly available through a GitHub repository (see Code availability). We hope that this work will facilitate future explorations in cancer biology and promote the development of therapeutic agents to manipulate the complex TME.

Industry observers note that to systematically analyse scRNA-seq cancer studies in the public domain, we evaluated all datasets published from January 2014 (when scRNA-seq was first described69) to July 2025. We only included studies using droplet-based methods, which have emerged as the dominant scRNA-seq approach, to minimize potential technique-specific artefacts when analysing integrated data70. Separate queries were evaluated independently for human and mouse datasets in the two largest public scRNA-seq repositories: the GEO71, managed by the National Institutes of Health (NIH), and ArrayExpress72, run by the European Bioinformatics Institute (EBI). Datasets that were specific to either blood or central nervous system cancers, or that failed to meet specific data architecture requirements (see Fig. 1a), were excluded from our analysis. We also excluded studies that removed stromal cells to ensure that these comparatively understudied cell populations were appropriately represented in the final atlas.

Our final comprehensive human TME atlas comprises 2,855 total samples from 190 scRNA-seq datasets. Our mouse atlas contains 526 total samples from 68 scRNA-seq datasets. Both human and mouse integrated TME atlases were generated (separately) using the following steps:.

Comprehensive curation of all publicly available cancer scRNA-seq datasets (Extended Data Fig. 1a).

Processing, filtering and quality control for individual scRNA-seq datasets (Extended Data Fig. 1b).

Disk/memory read optimization using the R package BPCells73,74 (Extended Data Fig. 1c,d).

Sketch-based sampling and integration across datasets using three independent approaches to reduce batch effects: Harmony, FastMNN or scVI75,76,77 (Extended Data Figs. 1e and 2a–f and Supplementary Fig. 1a–d).

Supervised annotation and filtering using a combination of canonical marker genes, estimated copy number variation (inferCNV, v1.14.2)78, SingleR79 and scATOMIC27 into seven broad cell types: epithelial, fibroblast, endothelial, mural, nerve, lymphoid and myeloid (Extended Data Fig. 1f and Supplementary Fig. 2).

It has been revealed that initial pooling of all cells that had been assigned to a given cell type by any one of the three approaches, permitting overlapping annotations (that is, the same cell being initially assigned to more than one cell type; Extended Data Fig. 1g).

Iterative removal of ‘misassigned’ cells through re-normalization, re-finding of variable features, re-scaling of data, re-performing of PCA, re-integration using Harmony (see the section ‘Selection of Harmony for downstream integration’ below for justification of this selection), re-clustering and re-annotation to generate the final ‘pure’ atlases for fibroblast, endothelial, mural, nerve, lymphoid and myeloid cells (Extended Data Fig. 1h), followed by final annotation of each population (Fig. 2d–i, Extended Data Fig. 1i,j and Supplementary Tables 6 and 7).

Generation of the final pan-cancer, all-cells TME human and mouse atlases.

Cross-species integration of human and mouse TME atlases.

These steps are described in detail in the following sections.

Recent findings suggest that publicly available human and mouse cancer scRNA-seq datasets were identified by searching two functional genomics databases: GEO and ArrayExpress (Extended Data Fig. 1a). The following search terms were used:.

Human GEO: (‘cancer’ OR ‘tumor’ OR ‘tumour’ OR ‘*carcinoma*’) AND ((‘single cell*’ OR ‘single-cell*’ OR ‘scRNA*’ OR ‘sc-RNA*’) OR (‘single nuc*’ OR ‘single-nuc*’ OR ‘snRNA*’ OR ‘sn-RNA*’)) AND 2014/01:2025/07[Publication Date] AND ‘Homo sapiens’[organism] AND ‘expression profiling by high throughput sequencing’[DataSet Type].

Mouse GEO: (‘cancer’ OR ‘tumor’ OR ‘tumour’ OR ‘*carcinoma*’) AND ((‘single cell*’ OR ‘single-cell*’ OR ‘scRNA*’ OR ‘sc-RNA*’) OR (‘single nuc*’ OR ‘single-nuc*’ OR ‘snRNA*’ OR ‘sn-RNA*’)) AND 2014/01:2025/07[Publication Date] AND ‘Mus musculus’[organism] AND ‘expression profiling by high throughput sequencing’[DataSet Type].

ArrayExpress: (‘cancer’ OR ‘tumor’ OR ‘tumour’ OR ‘*carcinoma*’) AND ((‘single cell*’ OR ‘single-cell*’ OR ‘scRNA*’ OR ‘sc-RNA*’) OR (‘single nuc*’ OR ‘single-nuc*’ OR ‘snRNA*’ OR ‘sn-RNA*’)).

A total of 2,168 human and 1,807 mouse datasets were manually screened to identify datasets that met the study inclusion criteria: (1) datasets must contain at least three scRNA-seq samples from primary tumour or non-malignant tissue samples; (2) the scRNA-seq platform must be droplet based (for example, 10X Genomics, Drop-seq, among others); (3) the cancer type must be a non-central nervous system, solid-organ tumour; and (4) the scRNA-seq sample must include at least some stromal cells. The mouse datasets were further screened to meet two additional inclusion criteria: (1) the tumour model must be either a genetically engineered mouse model or an orthotopic cancer cell line mouse model; and (2) the mouse bearing the tumour must not have received treatment. A total of 210 human scRNA-seq datasets and 79 mouse scRNA-seq datasets met these inclusion criteria (Extended Data Fig. 1a).

According to recent reports, data for each dataset were downloaded from their public repositories and converted into base Seurat objects using the functions read10X, read10X_h5, ReadMtx + CreateSeuratObject or read.table + CreateSeuratObject in R (v4.2.2). Each newly created Seurat object (corresponding to a single scRNA-seq sample) was then populated with the relevant sample-level meta-data. This was accomplished by first constructing a single large.csv file containing: the sample name, study name, organ, cancer, site (that is, tumour, tumour-adjacent or non-cancer) and FACS-sorting strategy (if any). For human samples, additional clinical meta-data — including patient age, sex, tumour clinical stage and treatment response — were recorded if available. For all mouse samples, the precise tumour model (for example, MMTV-PyMT) and tumour model type (for example, genetically engineered mouse model) were also recorded. These meta-data were manually collected from the corresponding database entries and articles across all 2,855 human samples and all 526 mouse samples.

Once populated with the above meta-data, samples were then analysed individually for quality control using the Seurat single-cell analysis pipeline (v4.9.9.9050)73. To ensure comparability across datasets, ENSEMBL transcript IDs and gene synonyms were converted to human or mouse gene symbols using biomaRt (v2.56), and only genes found in the human or mouse reference genome GRCh38.p14 or GRCm39 were retained. Afterwards, the raw count matrices for each dataset were confirmed to contain only integer values. Low-quality cells with nFeature_RNA ≤ 200 or nFeature_RNA ≥ 20% mitochondrial reads were then filtered out80 (Extended Data Fig. 1b). To remove potential doublets, data from individual samples were separately exported to Python using the writeH5AD function from the zellkonverter R package, followed by application of the Scrublet function from the Scrublet package81 and exported back to R. Cells ascribed as ‘doublets’ by scrublet using the default parameters were then removed. Finally, all samples from each dataset were merged and ‘flattened’ (using the JoinLayers function) into single Seurat objects for downstream analysis.

Given the large number of cells (more than 10 million), we used the BPCells package in R to abstract our sparse data matrices using bit-packing compression to minimize disk read/write requirements74 (Extended Data Fig. 1c). All subsequent operations were performed using objects in ‘BPCells format’, with conversion back into memory as dgCMatrix objects only when explicitly required (for example, R functions such as FindAllMarkers, as well as conversion to anndata objects for Python analyses). Conversion into BPCells objects was performed at the per-study level.

Recent findings suggest that the human and mouse datasets were separately integrated following the same steps: using Seurat (v4.9.9.9050) on study-level objects, the raw RNA counts were log normalized, and the top 2,000 variable features (highly variable genes) were identified. To improve the computational efficiency of analysing datasets spanning millions of cells, we selected a representative sketch of 1,000 cells per dataset based on the leverage scores calculated for each cell73 (Extended Data Fig. 1d). Using the sketched datasets, variable features were re-identified, expression levels were scaled and PCA was performed (npcs = 30). Next, integration of the sketched data was performed. Given that there is an element of stochasticity to any one method for integration and downstream analyses, which may result in the misclassification of a given individual cell35,79, we initially applied three distinct integration approaches in Seurat: Harmony, scVI and FastMNN (Extended Data Fig. 1e). The batch key for this integration was ‘study’, and no covariate regression was performed for any of the three methods. After each integration approach, UMAP dimensionality reduction was performed (dims = 1:30, min.dist = 0.001), neighbours were found (dims = 1:30) and initial clusters were identified (resolution varied based on dataset). The integration results and clusters from the sketched dataset were then projected onto the full dataset (Supplementary Fig. 2). All steps were performed using Seurat functions (NormalizeData, FindVariableFeatures, SketchData, ScaleData, RunPCA, IntegrateLayers, RunUMAP, FindNeighbours and FindClusters) with default parameters, except as mentioned above.

Distinct cell types in each of the Harmony, scVI and FastMNN atlases were identified and grouped into seven broad categories using canonical marker genes in conjunction with SingleR79, scATOMIC27, EnrichR82 and inferCNV78 (Supplementary Fig. 2). The predominant markers for each population were: epithelial cells (EPCAM), fibroblasts (PDGFRA), endothelial cells (PECAM1 (also known as CD31)), mural cells (RGS5), lymphoid cells (CD19 and CD3E), myeloid cells (CD14) and nerve cells (PLP1; Extended Data Fig. 1f).

To separately generate pan-cancer atlases for human and mouse CAFs, cells identified as fibroblasts by any of the Harmony, scVI or FastMNN algorithms were extracted in silico for further analysis (Extended Data Fig. 1g).

Using Seurat (v4.9.9.9050) and BPCells74, each cell type (for example, endothelial cells) was split by dataset, the raw RNA counts were log normalized, the top 2,000 variable features (highly variable genes) were identified, expression levels were scaled and PCA (npcs = 30) was performed. Next, integration of the data was performed using Harmony alone (see justification provided in the section ‘Selection of Harmony for downstream integration’). UMAP dimensionality reduction was performed (dims = 1:30, min.dist = 0.001), neighbours were found (dims = 1:30) and clusters were identified. Distinct cell types were annotated using the top 100 marker genes for each cluster, and contaminating non-endothelial clusters were removed. This computational pipeline was iterated four total times to generate the final human pan-cancer endothelial cell atlas and four total times to generate the final mouse pan-cancer endothelial cell atlas (Extended Data Fig. 1h,i). The specific details for the, as an example, human endothelial cell in silico ‘isolation’ are contained within Supplementary Fig. 3. Each subpopulation in the final human and mouse endothelial cell atlases were annotated in a semi-supervised manner using SingleR79, scATOMIC27 and canonical endothelial markers (PECAM1,  VWF and CDH5).

The human and mouse pan-cancer fibroblast, mural, nerve, lymphoid and myeloid cell atlases were similarly generated by including cells identified to be the given cell type by any of the three algorithms. The computational pipeline was iterated six, five, four, five and three times to generate the human endothelial, mural, nerve, lymphoid and myeloid cell atlases, respectively. Similarly, the computational pipeline was iterated three, three, two, four and four times to generate the mouse endothelial, mural, nerve, lymphoid and myeloid cell atlases, respectively. The subpopulations in the cell-type atlases were annotated as above (Extended Data Fig. 1j). Downstream analyses were not performed on epithelial cells due to the challenges in distinguishing epithelial from tumour cells in cancers of epithelial origin. It is worth noting that our approach does not explicitly account for the potential presence of ambient RNA within the droplets used to extract transcriptional profiles83. Unfortunately, owing to the format of most publicly available scRNA-seq datasets (lacking ‘unfiltered’ count matrices), robust methods for ambient RNA correction such as CellBender84 or SoupX85 could not be applied.

The human cell subpopulation annotations and mouse subpopulation annotations from the six separate cell-type atlases were subsequently mapped back onto the respective all-cells atlases. Cells labelled as epithelial cells in the initial broad categorization in (5) were annotated as epithelial cells. Cells that were filtered out through the iterative cleaning steps were removed. In total, the final human TME atlas had 45 cell populations, and the final mouse TME atlas had 44 cell populations (Fig. 2a and Extended Data Fig. 9a).

To evaluate the conservation of cell subpopulations within the TME between humans and mice, the human and mouse cell-type atlases were integrated for each of six primary TME cell types in Seurat (v4.9.9.9050). To perform this integration, orthologue transformation was performed using the convert_mouse_to_human_symbols function in the NicheNet R package (v2.0.4)86 to convert the mouse gene names in the mouse atlases into human orthologue gene names. The six human cell-type atlases were then merged separately with the corresponding mouse cell-type atlas. For each of the combined human–mouse atlases, Seurat (v4.9.9.9050) was used to split the object by dataset, normalize data, find variable features, scale expression levels, perform PCA (npcs = 30), integrate the data using Harmony and perform UMAP dimensionality reduction (dims = 1:30, min.dist = 0.001). To assess human–mouse conservation of cell types, the UMAP results were plotted such that each cell was coloured by the cell-type annotation from the respective human or mouse cell-type atlas (Fig. 5a–f). To assess the quality of this cross-species analysis, we used two approaches. First, we developed a correlation matrix based on co-incidence among underlying clusters (Fig. 5a–f, right); second, we applied anchor-based label transfer to map mouse annotations onto human cells. The latter was performed by separately applying SCTransform in Seurat to both mouse and human objects for each of the principal cell types used in Fig. 5a–f. Then, FindTransferAnchors was applied with dimensions of 1:30, reduction = ‘pca’, followed by TransferData with dimensions of 1:30. No changes to other default parameters were made. Heatmaps of overlap were generated using ggplot2 (Supplementary Fig. 24a–f).

It has been revealed that harmony was selected as the approach for all subsequent downstream integration (beyond the initial first-pass using all three approaches) based on its performance in biological conservation and batch metrics using scIB35 (Supplementary Table 5). For this analysis, Seurat objects integrated by each of the three approaches (Harmony, scVI and FastMNN) were converted into SingleCellExperiment objects using the SingleCellExperiment library. The resulting objects were imported into Python using the anndata2ri package. Individual metrics were then calculated using the scib.metrics function set within scIB.

Sources indicate that the human TME atlas was used to perform six downstream analyses: (1) cell subpopulation enrichment analysis, (2) SCENIC analysis, (3) scMetabolism analysis, (4) TCGA survival analysis, (5) CellChat analysis, and (6) NicheNet analysis. The methods for each of these six analyses are detailed below.

The relative enrichment of each cell subpopulation in the human scRNA-seq TME atlas was directly calculated for three clinically relevant meta-data categories: between samples from non-malignant tissue versus tumour; between early-stage (I and II) and late-stage (III and IV) tumours; and between treatment responsive and non-responsive tumours. The relative enrichment of each cell subpopulation in the mouse scRNA-seq TME atlas was directly calculated between non-malignant versus tumour tissue. These meta-data were annotated in a consistent manner for each scRNA-seq sample if available in the original article. To calculate relative enrichment for each cell subpopulation, the percentage of cells in each cell subpopulation (for example, ISG15+ iCAFs) out of all cells in the broader cell type (for example, fibroblast) was calculated for each sample. To avoid unstable proportion estimates from sparsely represented samples, any sample contributing 30 or fewer cells to a given parent cell type was excluded from the analysis of the subpopulations of that cell type. This criterion was applied independently for each parent lineage, so the number of samples contributing to a given comparison depends on that lineage and was substantially smaller than the total number of samples in the cohort; within a lineage, the same set of samples contributes to every constituent subpopulation. The exact n for every comparison is reported in the corresponding figure legends and in Supplementary Tables 8 and 13.

Statistical significance for cell subpopulation enrichment was determined using a two-sided weighted Welch t-test for two independent samples (wtd.t.test, weights R package (v1.0.4), with samedata = FALSE), in which the unit of replication was the individual scRNA-seq sample and the tested quantity was the per-sample subpopulation proportion. To account for highly variable single-cell capture rates, sample weights were assigned as the square root of the number of cells per sample. Degrees of freedom were obtained by the Welch–Satterthwaite approximation and are therefore non-integer. Separately, the weighted standard errors of the group means that define the plotted error bars were computed using the Kish effective sample size, neff = (Σw)2/Σw2, which downweights the contribution of samples with disproportionately large cell numbers. Because the cell subpopulations are nested within parent cell types, Benjamini–Hochberg adjustment was applied separately within each parent lineage, so that each family of tests corresponds to the set of subpopulations that partition a single parent cell type; Benjamini–Hochberg adjusted P values computed across all subpopulations simultaneously are additionally reported for completeness. Full statistical outputs for every comparison, including the exact n per group, weighted group means and standard errors, fold enrichment with its 95% confidence interval (obtained by the delta method on the log scale), the t-statistic, the degrees of freedom, and exact raw and adjusted P values, are provided in Supplementary Tables 8 and 13.

Recent findings suggest that SCENIC87 was used to calculate the area under the recovery curve (AUC) for the enrichment of regulons in human scRNA-seq. Seurat objects were generated with AUC scores and clustered by running the standard Seurat pipeline. Differentially expressed regulons were identified by running the FindAllMarkers function and plotted using the standard DimPlot function (Extended Data Fig. 5a–d).

To evaluate whether specific cell populations may be correlated with differences in metabolic programs, we used the scMetabolism package in R88. Seurat objects for all pooled stromal cell populations (Extended Data Fig. 5e) or individually separate Seurat objects (Extended Data Fig. 5f–h) were evaluated using the sc.metabolism.Seurat function with parameters: method = ‘AUCell’, imputation = F, ncores = 2 and metabolism.type = ‘KEGG’. Using default input pathways of ‘glycolysis/gluconeogenesis’, ‘oxidative phosphorylation’ and ‘citrate cycle (TCA cycle)’, metabolic plots in (Extended Data Fig. 5e–h) were generated using the DotPlot.metabolism function for each population grouping.

Bulk RNA-seq data from TCGA2 were used to orthogonally calculate the relative enrichment of each cell subpopulation in tumour-adjacent versus tumour samples and to assess the effect of each cell subpopulation on patient survival. TCGA dataset included 9,880 primary tumour and 740 tumour-adjacent samples across 31 solid tumour types, and the dataset was downloaded using TCGAbiolinks (v3.18)2. To deconvolve TCGA bulk RNA-seq data, we first generated a downsampled scRNA-seq reference that contained 1,000 randomly chosen cells for each of the cell subpopulations from the human TME atlas. Using this downsampled scRNA-seq reference, bulk deconvolution using CIBERSORTx with S-mode batch correction was performed for each of the 31 TCGA solid-organ cancer types. The output of bulk deconvolution is an estimate of the percentage of each cell subpopulation in each sample. For each cell subpopulation, the mean and standard error of the cell subpopulation proportions in tumour and tumour-adjacent samples were calculated. The relative enrichment in tumour-adjacent versus tumour samples was computed as the ratio between the two groups (Supplementary Fig. 6a).

The CIBERSORTx cell subpopulation proportion estimates from the tumour samples were additionally used to assess the effect of each cell subpopulation on patient survival. First, for each cell subpopulation, patient tumour samples for each cancer type were stratified into two groups based on the relative proportion of the cell subpopulation. For instance, patients whose tumour samples had a proportion greater than the mean estimated proportion for that subpopulation were considered high-abundance groups, and conversely, patients whose tumour samples had a proportion less than the mean estimated proportion were considered low-abundance groups. Cox regression analysis implemented with the survcomp R package was then used to estimate hazard ratios between high and low expressors for each cancer type by using survival time clinical meta-data from TCGA. A pan-cancer hazard ratio for each cell subpopulation was then estimated by calculating the inverse-variance weighted average of the hazard ratios from each of the 31 cancer types (Supplementary Fig. 6b).

Recent findings suggest that to correct for multiple hypothesis testing, Benjamini–Hochberg adjusted P values were calculated for all comparisons. Full statistical outputs, including fold enrichment or hazard ratio, weighted standard errors and adjusted P values for all clinical group comparisons, are provided in Supplementary Table 9.

Sources indicate that cellChat (v1.5.0)89 was used to analyse putative cell–cell communication networks among cell subpopulations in our human TME atlas. To perform CellChat, the associated TME Seurat object was first downsampled to only include 100,000 randomly chosen cells, with at least 100 cells per cell subpopulation. The raw counts corresponding to these downsampled data (and their associated meta-data) were extracted from the initial Seurat object and used to populate a new CellChat object. Labels for the non-nerve TME subpopulations were used as groupings. This object was processed through the standard CellChat pipeline, followed by network centrality analysis for pathways of interest (Fig. 4a, Extended Data Fig. 7a,c and Supplementary Fig. 15a).

NicheNet (v2.0.4)86 was used to provide orthogonal support for cell–cell communication networks predicted by CellChat. Seurat objects were downsampled to 100,000 randomly chosen cells (at least 100 per subpopulation), and then fed into NicheNet using sender and receiver populations (as described below) to assess interactions. Regulatory potential heatmaps were generated to visualize these interactions, systematically displaying prioritized sender ligands on the y axis and their regulatory potential against predicted target genes on the x axis. Specifically, this framework was applied to evaluate signalling from: (1) T CD8+GZMB+ cells to ISG15+ iCAFs (IFNγ signalling, Fig. 4b); (2) dendritic cells to ISG15+ iCAFs (MIF signalling; Supplementary Fig. 15b–d); (3) macrophage–monocyte to ESM1+ tip cells (VEGF signalling; Extended Data Fig. 7b); and (4) mural cells to ESM1+ tip cells (Extended Data Fig. 7d).

Formalin-fixed, paraffin-embedded (FFPE) tumour and tumour-adjacent tissue blocks were acquired from the Stanford Department of Pathology for seven PDAC, three PTC and three CRC specimens. Immunofluorescence staining was performed on 8-µm histological sections. For immunofluorescence staining, slides were immersed for 10 min in pre-warmed sodium citrate buffer (10 mM, pH 6.0) for antigen retrieval, and slides were blocked for 1 h in Power Block (BioGenex). For PDGFRα–HLA-DR co-localization, slides were incubated overnight at 4 °C with the following primary antibodies: anti-human PDGFRα rabbit monoclonal antibody (3174, CST; clone D1E1E) and anti-human HLA-DR mouse monoclonal antibody (327002, BioLegend; clone LN3). Slides were then incubated for 1 h with the following secondary antibodies: Alexa Fluor 647-conjugated donkey anti-rabbit polyclonal antibody (A-31573, Invitrogen) and Alexa Fluor 555-conjugated donkey anti-mouse polyclonal antibody (A-31570, Invitrogen). Finally, slides were mounted using Fluoromount-G mounting medium with DAPI (00-4959-52, Invitrogen). Fluorescent images at ×20 magnification were acquired with a Leica SP8 inverted confocal microscope.

CODEX/Phenocycler, a highly multiplexed immunofluorescence technique, was previously used to quantify the spatial expression of 30 proteins for 3 PDAC FFPE histological sections by our laboratory90. The CODEX panel assessed expression of several fibroblast markers (αSMA and COL1), an apCAF marker (HLA-DR), immune cell markers (CD11c, CD20, CD68, CD8 and CD4) and epithelial/tumour cell markers (E-cadherin and pan-cytokeratin (CK)). Separately, a fibre quantification algorithm developed by our laboratory was previously used to quantify the matrix architecture from 85 FFPE PDAC specimens91. In brief, 8-µm haematoxylin and eosin (H&E)-stained histological sections were imaged at ×40, and 354,838 200 × 200 µm image tiles were programmatically generated. Afterwards, the histological architecture was quantified for each tile by examining 147 fibre features, and UMAP dimensionality reduction and trajectory analysis using Monocle3 were performed to assign pseudotime values to individual H&E tiles, with high average matrix pseudotime for a given patient correlating with worse patient survival. To examine the matrix architecture in the CODEX sections, 8-µm histological sections consecutive to the CODEX sections were previously stained with H&E, and 200 × 200 µm image tiles were previously analysed using the fibre quantification algorithm. The H&E tiles were spatially aligned with the CODEX sections using GIMP to generate a spatial map of matrix pseudotime for each of the three CODEX sections. In this present study, the CODEX Multiplex Analysis Viewer was used to visualize the multiplex immunofluorescence staining for 11 protein markers in regions of high and low matrix pseudotime in three PDAC CODEX sections. Spindle-like HLA-DR+αSMA+COL1+CD68−CD11c−CD20−CD8−CD4−E-cadherin−pan-CK−CD31− cells were identified by inspection.

To provide further validation for our immunofluorescence and CODEX observations above, we used a publicly Xenium dataset from the 10X Genomics website: Pancreatic Cancer with Xenium Human Multi-Tissue and Cancer Panel (https://www.10xgenomics.com/datasets/pancreatic-cancer-with-xenium-human-multi-tissue-and-cancer-panel-1-standard; dataset listing: https://www.10xgenomics.com/datasets?query=Xenium). The scRNA-seq reference was constructed by selecting cell populations from our initial global populations with our fibroblast subtyping. For deconvolution, the NiCo 1.1.0 pipeline63 was implemented as recommended by filtering and normalizing the reference dataset and Xenium ST datasets, finding commonly shared genes, performing SCTransform from Scanpy, and Leiden clustering the Xenium data at a resolution of 0.7. Then, the find_anchor_cells_between_ref_and_query and nico_based_annotation function was run to find anchors between the reference and Xenium ST datasets with a spatial dispersion cut-off of 0.15. Colocalization of genes (transcripts) and populations (labelled cells) were then used to generate the accompanying figures.

Recent findings suggest that primary CAFs were isolated using the Miltenyi Biotec Tumor Dissociation Kit (130-095-929) from one fresh pancreatic PDAC surgical specimen under an institutional review board (IRB)-approved protocol, with informed consent obtained preoperatively under Stanford’s IRB-65893 (ref. 92). The donor was one male patient. No established or immortalized cell lines were used in this study; fibroblast identity follows from the primary outgrowth isolation protocol of ref. 92 and was not separately confirmed by marker analysis. The cultures were not tested for mycoplasma contamination. Isolated CAFs were cultured for four passages in DMEM/F-12 with GlutaMAX (10565018, Gibco), 10% FBS (16000044, Gibco), 1% antibiotic–antimycotic (B22110, R&D) and 0.2% primocin (ant-pm-05, InvivoGen). Passage 4 cells (105 cells per replicate; n = 3 replicates per condition) were allowed to adhere for 12 h, after which cells were treated for 24 h with control media, recombinant human IFNγ (20 ng ml−1; 285-IF, R&D) or LPS (100 ng ml−1; tlrl-eblps, InvivoGen). Cells from a single passage-4 pool were split into nine plates, which were not further passaged, and each plate was then treated and sequenced independently (three plates per condition). RNA was then extracted using TRIzol (15596026, Invitrogen). Nine RNA-seq libraries were prepared with the NEBNext Ultra II Directional RNA Library Prep Kit for Illumina (E7760, NEB) following the manufacturer’s protocol for the NEBNext rRNA Depletion Kit v2 (human/mouse/rat) (E7400L, NEB).

Sources indicate that for each library, 50 ng of each replicate was used as input. During the adaptor ligation step, Singular Genomics Universal Library Prep Adapter (#700110) was used to adapt libraries to be sequenced on the Singular Genomics G4 sequencer. PCR enrichment of adaptor-ligated DNA was performed for 12 cycles. No index reads were performed (read 1, 75 bp; read 2, 75 bp; no index cycles), as each library was sequenced in a dedicated lane. All RNA-seq libraries were sequenced on a G4 sequencer instrument for paired-end 2 × 75 bp sequencing, across three sequencing runs performed on the same day, with a single library sequenced per lane (nine lanes in total).

In a recent development, bulk RNA-seq data were extracted from the sequencer as per-lane fastq files, one library per lane and transferred to the Stanford SCG server. Individual fastq files were aligned to the human GRCh37-hg19 reference genome using TopHat (v2.0.13), resulting in nine counts matrices (n = 3 biological replicates for each of the three experimental groups). These data were read into R using the base read.delimn function, were merged into a single matrix using cbind, and then were annotated according to sample name, replicate and condition. To compute the top differentially expressed genes between each pair of conditions, counts per million (CPM) normalization was first performed on the counts matrices using the cpm function. A gene threshold of at least 2 samples with at least 0.5 CPM was used, resulting in 26,363 genes being preserved for downstream analyses. PCA was performed using prcomp, and the log-transformed PCA data were plotted using autoplot. Differentially expressed genes between groups were determined using DESeq2 (v1.38.4), with its functions calcNormFactors, esimateCommonDisp, estimageGLMTrededDisp, estimatedTagwiseDisp, DESeq and lfcShrink. Volcano plots of the resulting resLFC objects were then generated using EnhancedVolcano (v1.13.2). The biological coefficient of variation was calculated using plotBCV (Supplementary Fig. 16a). EnrichR analyses were performed on the top 200 genes upregulated following treatment with either IFNγ or LPS (Supplementary Fig. 16b,c).

It has been revealed that to generate a signature for ISG15+ and CXCL8+ iCAFs, the top 50 genes defining the ISG15+ iCAF and CXCL8+ iCAF subpopulations were first identified using the FindAllMarkers function. To calculate a signature score for each iCAF subpopulation, the expression values of the 50 marker genes in each sample was examined. First, to equally weight the 50 marker genes, row-wise normalization of the counts matrix was performed (for example, Vi,j = Vi,j/Σ(Vi)). Then, to calculate the signature score for each iCAF subpopulation, the normalized expression values for the 50 marker genes were summed for each sample. Standard deviation and standard error were then computed based on the dispersal of cluster signature scores for biological replicates in each condition.

According to recent reports, we examined four large, recent TME atlases published by Nofech-Mozes et al.27, Nieto et al.28, Kang et al.20 and Han et al.21. For each atlas, we downloaded the corresponding full atlas object from its respective repository and converted to SingleCellExperiment objects. Large datasets were downsampled to 50,000 cells. The scTME toolkit was then applied to blindly annotate each cell separately within the query dataset according to cell populations from our TME atlas. The resulting predictive scTME annotations were then compared against the annotations provided for that specific dataset, and heatmaps were generated based on co-incidence.

Using this large atlas, we developed a newly introduced R package, scTME, that utilizes population-level data to provide probability estimates for the annotation of cells within a given cluster in a candidate dataset. This package utilizes many of the classification functions within the SingleR toolkit79, which is a prerequisite for scTME. The program takes a single required input:.

A query dataset (obj), supplied as either a Seurat object or a SingleCellExperiment object of genes (g) × cells (c) dimensions. Data that have not been log normalized are normalized automatically.

All remaining inputs are optional.

Sources indicate that an optional reference dataset (ref). When omitted, the integrated human TME atlas distributed with the package is used.

According to recent reports, an optional vector of cluster labels (clusters), of (1 × c) dimensions, or the name of a metadata column containing them, corresponding to the cell groupings over which the object will be evaluated. When supplied, annotation was performed at the level of these groupings and the assigned label was propagated to each constituent cell; when omitted, each cell was annotated individually.

Industry observers note that an optional factor (level) that was set to 2 by default, corresponding to the 45 subpopulations defined in Fig. 2a,d–i. It can alternatively be switched to one, in which case the output will correspond to the seven broad cell types defined in Fig. 2a.

An optional parameter, label.col, naming the column of reference metadata from which labels were drawn, for use when a custom reference is supplied.

An optional threshold, max.cells (default 50,000), above which the data will be randomly subsampled to a final object with the number of cells equal to max.cells.

An optional parameter, return.details (default = FALSE), which will output the scoring matrices in addition to the final cell annotations.

A (1 × c dimensional) label vector corresponding to the annotations assigned to each cell, based on their original input grouping and the output annotated to each grouping.

In a recent development, A scoring matrix corresponding to the probabilities assessed to each group-level assignment. This is only returned if return.details = TRUE. If so, these two outputs are returned as a list.

Details of the code itself can be found within the GitHub documentation (https://github.com/michaeljanuszyk/scTME) and it can be installed using the devtools library in R with: install_github(‘michaeljanuszyk/scTME’).

Original illustrations were drawn using an Apple iPad Pro and Apple Pencil 2.0 in Procreate (v5.2.7) software. Post-editing adjustments of parameters such as brightness, contrast and saturation were applied in Adobe Photoshop (v23.4.2). Finally, text and object overlays were added to the figures using Biorender (https://biorender.com; see relevant figure legends for licenses).

No statistical method was used to predetermine sample size. For the meta-analysis, sample size was determined by the number of published scRNA-seq datasets meeting the inclusion criteria defined in Fig. 1a. No data were excluded from the analyses other than by the pre-specified dataset-level and cell-level quality control criteria described above. No randomization was used. For the meta-analysis, all published datasets meeting the inclusion criteria were included, so no allocation step arose. For the in vitro experiments, the replicate cultures were assigned to the control, IFNγ and LPS conditions without randomization and handled in parallel. Unless stated otherwise in the corresponding figure legend, all statistical tests were two-sided and all P values were adjusted for multiple comparisons using the Benjamini–Hochberg procedure. Exact adjusted P values are reported in Supplementary Tables 8–10 and 13.

According to recent reports, cell subpopulation enrichment analyses (Fig. 3a–c and Supplementary Fig. 21) were performed using a two-sided weighted Welch t-test for two independent samples, in which the unit of replication was the individual scRNA-seq sample and sample weights were equal to the square root of the number of cells per sample, with Welch–Satterthwaite degrees of freedom. Within each parent lineage, these analyses were restricted to samples contributing more than 30 cells to that lineage. Sample numbers therefore differ between lineages and are stated per lineage in the legend of Fig. 3 and for every individual comparison in Supplementary Table 8.

In a recent development, across all lineages, the number of contribution samples are 859–1,777 (Fig. 3a), 311–658 (Fig. 3b) and 48–108 (Fig. 3c) samples per parent cell lineage. Exact values per lineage are given in Supplementary Table 8. No statistic reported in this study is derived from fewer than three biologically independent samples per group. Within a given lineage, the same set of samples contributes to every constituent subpopulation. Benjamini–Hochberg adjustment was applied separately within each parent lineage. No statistics were derived from any comparison with fewer than three biologically independent samples per group. TCGA deconvolution analyses (Supplementary Fig. 6) used n = 9,880 primary tumour and 740 normal samples across 31 solid tumour types, with hazard ratios estimated by Cox regression and pooled across cancer types by inverse-variance weighting.

According to recent reports, immunofluorescence co-staining for PDGFRα and HLA-DR (Fig. 3d) was performed on n = 7 biologically independent PDAC, n = 3 biologically independent CRC and n = 3 biologically independent PTC specimens from patients, together with matched tumour-adjacent tissue. Each specimen was stained and imaged once, and comparable staining patterns were observed across all specimens of a given tumour type; the images shown are representative. CODEX analyses (Fig. 3f–h) were performed on n = 3 biologically independent PDAC specimens, each analysed once within a single multiplexed imaging run, with comparable findings in each; the images shown are representative. Spindle-like HLA-DR+αSMA+COL1+ cells negative for tumour and other immune cell markers were identified by visual inspection. Investigators were not blinded to matrix pseudotime region assignment, which was determined programmatically by the fibre quantification algorithm before inspection.

Recent findings suggest that the in vitro CAF stimulation experiment (Fig. 4d–h and Supplementary Fig. 16) was performed with n = 3 replicate cultures per condition, split from a single primary PDAC CAF isolate and treated and sequenced independently. Differential expression between conditions was assessed using DESeq2 (v1.38.4) with a two-sided Wald test and Benjamini–Hochberg adjustment across the 26,363 genes passing the expression threshold. iCAF signature scores (Fig. 4g,h) are presented as mean ± s.d. of the three replicate cultures, with individual replicate values overlaid, and were compared using two-sided unpaired Student’s t-tests (equal variances assumed). Investigators were not blinded during the in vitro experiments, as all readouts were quantitative and derived computationally from sequencing data.

Industry observers note that FFPE tumour and tumour-adjacent tissue specimens were obtained from the pathology repository of the Stanford University Department of Pathology. No human participants were recruited for the purpose of this study, and all sample collection was performed with the approval of the IRB of the Stanford University School of Medicine. All tissue specimens were coded and de-identified before further processing, in accordance with patient privacy regulations. No animal experiments were performed in this study; all mouse single-cell RNA-seq data analysed here are previously published and were generated under the approvals reported in their original publications. The fresh PDAC surgical specimen used for primary CAF isolation was collected under Stanford IRB protocol IRB-65893, with informed consent obtained preoperatively. All previously published single-cell RNA-seq datasets analysed in this study were obtained from public repositories and were generated under the approvals reported in their original publications.

Further information on research design is available in the Nature Portfolio Reporting Summary linked to this article.

According to recent reports, all previously published human and mouse scRNA-seq datasets analysed in this study are publicly available from the GEO and ArrayExpress; the accession code for each of the 258 constituent datasets is listed in Supplementary Table 1. The bulk RNA-seq data generated in this study (nine libraries from primary human PDAC CAFs treated with control media, IFNγ or LPS) have been deposited in the GEO under accession code GSE348821 and are publicly available; the corresponding processed results are additionally enumerated in Supplementary Table 10. Bulk RNA-seq and associated clinical data from TCGA were obtained using TCGAbiolinks from the NCI Genomic Data Commons Data Portal (https://portal.gdc.cancer.gov/). The spatial transcriptomics data used for validation are the publicly available 10X Genomics dataset ‘pancreatic cancer with Xenium human multi-tissue and cancer panel’ (https://www.10xgenomics.com/datasets/pancreatic-cancer-with-xenium-human-multi-tissue-and-cancer-panel-1-standard). The four previously published atlases used for comparison were obtained from their respective repositories as cited in Methods. The integrated human and mouse TME atlases generated in this study can be browsed and queried (http://tmeatlas.stanford.edu), and have been deposited at Zenodo93 (https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23029384) as gene-by-cell count matrices in 10X Genomics HDF5 format, together with the per-cell sample and annotation metadata, and the Harmony and UMAP cell embeddings. Source data underlying Figs. 3a–c and 4d–h are provided in Supplementary Tables 8 and 10. All other data supporting the findings of this study are available within the paper and its Supplementary Information.

Industry observers note that the scTME R package developed in this study is publicly available on GitHub (https://github.com/michaeljanuszyk/scTME) and can be installed using the devtools library with install_github(‘michaeljanuszyk/scTME’). All custom code used for dataset curation, quality control, integration, annotation and downstream analysis in this study is available in the same repository, and the version of record used to generate the results reported here is archived at Zenodo94 (https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23027610). All other software used in this study is publicly available and is cited, with version numbers, in the Methods.

Schematic created in BioRender; Wang, H. https://biorender.com/w8x4pii (2026). b, Quality control metrics included ensuring that the number of unique genes per cell (nFeature_RNA) was > 200 and the fraction of mitochondrial reads was <20%. Cells with nFeature_RNA ≥ 95th percentile were also removed as a precaution against doublets. c, Data were then converted into an optimized read/write disk space using BPCells. d, To further streamline computation, all data were then sketched into representative 1,000-cell subsets on a per-study basis. e, The resulting data (12.8 M cells for human or 2.5 M cells for mouse) were then integrated on a per-study basis using three independent approaches (Harmony, scVI, FastMNN), resulting in three distinct clusterings and uniform manifold approximation and projection (UMAP) embeddings. f, Each of the three objects from e were annotated independently in a semi-supervised fashion using canonical markers in conjunction with the automated classification toolkits SingleR and scATOMIC, resulting in seven coarse cell type designations for each of the three distinct objects. g, For each of the six TME cell types (epithelial cells are excluded moving forward), separate and parallel computational pipelines were followed. This begins with pooling all cells designated as a given cell type (e.g., fibroblasts) by any of the three integration approaches, and creating a common object. h, Each cell type-specific object undergoes re-integration using study-specific batch keys, followed by normalization, scaling, principal component analysis (PCA), UMAP, clustering, and re-annotation to assess purity. Improperly classified cells are then removed, and this process of recursive cleaning is repeated until all cells are found to be of the correct cell type. i, Once all cells are found to be correctly classified, the final atlas for that cell type is annotated and final subpopulations are determined. j, As described above, the process from g to i is repeated→ separately for each of the primary six TME cell types in this atlas.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Tottenham winger Mykhailo Mudryk has blamed the Ukraine national team setup for the failed doping test that resulted in his lengthy suspension from football.

The 25-year-old, currently on loan from Chelsea, has spoken about the ordeal in an interview on the Ukrainian YouTube podcast Guest of Gordon, claiming that inadequate security and supplement procedures within the national team environment may have contributed to his positive test.

Mudryk tested positive for the prohibited substance meldonium in November 2024, triggering a suspension that kept him out of competitive football until July 2026.

The Ukrainian international has now described the devastating psychological impact of the situation and explained why he believes the substance could only have entered his body while he was in Ukraine.

Mudryk admitted that discovering he had tested positive for meldonium was one of the most difficult moments of his career.

The winger insisted that he had never knowingly taken the substance and struggled to understand how it could have entered his system.

Speaking on podcast, Mudryk noted:.

“It was a bolt from the blue. I couldn’t believe it [the positive doping test] was true… It was like falling off a skyscraper. In a dream you would hit the ground. In life, I just kept on falling. It hit me very hard, mentally….

“I had never heard of a drug like meldonium. It is a drug you can only get in Eastern Europe. It could only have got into my body in Ukraine. There is no such drug in England.

It has been revealed that “The Ukrainian national team has absolutely no security system… On the Ukrainian national team we have a nutritionist who hands us pills every couple of days before games. He brings us a little cup. Everyone has to take the pills that are in that cup.”.

Pressed point-blank on whether he blamed the national team for the positive result, Mudryk answered: “Yes, exactly”.

According to recent reports, ? Mykhailo Mudryk says he blames the Ukraine national team for his doping suspension in an interview with 'Guest of Gordon', a Ukranian podcast.

Sources indicate that "It was a bolt from the blue. I couldn’t believe it [the positive doping test] was true….

"It was like falling off a skyscraper.… pic.twitter.com/wQPAOIx1oT.

— Ben Jacobs (@JacobsBen) November 18, 2026.

The positive test cost Mudryk nearly two years of his prime, keeping him suspended from November 2024 until July 2026 before a successful appeal to the Court of Arbitration for Sport reduced an initial four-year sanction.

Banned from using Chelsea’s training facilities, Mudryk revealed he spent millions of pounds out of pocket on legal fees, private coaching, and physiotherapy to stay sharp.

With new Chelsea boss Xabi Alonso urging him to seek regular minutes elsewhere, Mudryk sealed a deadline-day season-long loan to Tottenham, which includes a £75 million buy option, reuniting with former Shakhtar Donetsk mentor Roberto De Zerbi.

Though an ankle injury suffered in training has restricted him to a single 17-minute substitute outing against Nottingham Forest so far, Mudryk is nearing full fitness and now has the ideal platform under De Zerbi to revive his Premier League career.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that two matchdays remain in the Apertura portion of the Liga MX season, and there's everything to play for, from the title down to the final playoff spots. CBS Sports Golazo Network will be the place to see plenty of the key action. Club America lead Chivas Guadalajara and Cruz Azul only on goal difference, while Atlas are also a surprise contender for the title, trailing by only two points. Club America may have the best attack in the league, with Henry Martin leading the line and getting back to his best, but a potentially tricky matchup with Pumas could cost them points.

Club America have lost only twice this season, but they have scuffled a bit and are winless in their last three, including a loss to Pachuca, who are led by the league's top scorer in the ageless Salomon Rondon. At the opposite end of the spectrum, the final four playoff spots are essentially up for grabs, as anyone currently fifth to 11th could be passed, and only four teams have been mathematically eliminated from playoff contention.

It has been revealed that technically, Puebla are done if anyone on 22 points secures a point, but even the fact that they have a chance in 14th place demonstrates how competitive this season has been. But it's also one that could bring quite a shock if the table ends as it is at the moment, with Monterrey on the outside looking in at the playoffs.

Sources indicate that date: Saturday, Nov. 7 | Time: 8 p.m. ETLocation: Estadio Nemesio Diez -- Toluca de Lerdo, MexicoLive stream: CBS Sports Golazo NetworkOdds: Toluca -170; Draw +340; Monterrey +360.

Traveling away to face Toluca, Rayados need all the points that they can get and then some. They haven't missed the playoffs since 2016, and despite being the third-highest-spending team, behind Atlas and Club America, there hasn't been much to show for it as Matias Almeyda's chaotic management follows the squad through the season. They have talent in the squad, but it's not all coming together all at once. This team is just as likely to win 4-2 as it is to lose by the same score, and that comes down to management, not talent.

It has been revealed that on talent, there's no reason for Monterrey to miss the playoffs, and having three of the top 15 scorers on their team highlights that this is an attack to be feared. It's anyone's guess if they'll actually get things together in time, but if it doesn't happen Saturday night, only 90 minutes will remain before missing the playoffs becomes reality for the club.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that "Skill" is very much a subjective term anyway, but this is especially true in football. A skilful defender and a skilful attacker may well be worthy of such a description, but what that term incorporates is changed entirely due to their positional differences. Generally, a player must have exceptional technical ability to be considered skilful, as many of the term's connotations relate to players who have wowed their opponents and on-watching fans with what they were able to do on the ball.

In a modern game where many metrics are ranked on quality based on statistics, "skill" is one of the few that can not be quantified. Goals or assists can indicate a player's productivity, but whether or not they are skilful is something that can be defined only by watching them, and seeing how they use the ball to benefit their team. So, with all of that being considered, which players within football over the years have displayed the highest levels of skill?

Industry observers note that sergio Busquets, as a defensive midfielder, probably would not be a name that jumps to everybody’s mind when asked who the most skilful players in football have been, and that is understandable, but his technical ability can not be understated. During his prime years with Barcelona, Busquets was an integral part of their success, his composure and class on the ball often going under the radar.

According to recent reports, pep Guardiola once referred to him as a player who could “solve any problem with his brain,” so strong and complex is his understanding of the game. Guardiola also feels that Busquets will make “an exceptional coach” upon retiring from football, high praise from one of history’s greatest gaffers.

One of the finest technicians of the Premier League era, Dimitar Berbatov quite rightly is regarded as one of the most skilful players ever, particularly for those English football fans who watched him light it up with both Tottenham and Manchester United. The Bulgarian possessed an exquisite first touch and incredibly quick feet for someone so tall, and his ability to beat a man using just his dribbling skills rather than any explosive pace made him elegant to watch.

The ultimate no.10, Juan Roman Riquelme was a supreme talent who made the ball talk with his incredible passing skills. Capable of threading the ball through the eye of a needle with both his instep and the outside of his foot, Riquelme was a devastating play-maker. The Argentine was also famed for his drag-backs, where he would lure a player in trying to tackle him, and then promptly move away from him, leaving them behind in the dust.

Sources indicate that one of the best two-footed players in football history, Santi Cazorla was so good with both feet that in a game against Watford at Vicarage Road, having lined up to take an outswinging corner with his right, teammate Laurent Koscielny whistled at him and got him to take an inswinger with his left. The former Arsenal star is beloved at the Emirates, and it is understandable.

Despite being a diminutive playmaker, Cazorla also had the fight to go with his skill, and his mazy runs from midfield - who can forget his iconic run from inside his own half against Manchester City at the Etihad - made him a joy to watch.

In terms of the greatest players in Premier League history, Eden Hazard is surely up there in the conversation. In terms of his peak performance and prime years, the Belgian completely lit up English football while with Chelsea, combining devastating skill with an incredible ability to finish from tight angles and holding defenders off.

At his best, Hazard could beat teams on his own, taking players out of the equation with a simple jink of his shoulder and his underrated strength.

One of the greatest midfielders in history, Andres Iniesta, is unsurprisingly on the list of the most skilful players in football history. The former Spain international was a key part of the Barcelona side that conquered all alongside Lionel Messi, while he was also instrumental in La Roja's triumphs in the EUROs and the World Cup - of course, he was the goal-scorer in the 1-0 win over the Netherlands in the latter tournament's final.

In a recent development, iniesta had an exquisite first touch and had the ball at his feet like it was simply glued to him. While he may not have been the quickest, there was no one quicker in the brain than the talented Spain star.

Though there will always be questions over his consistency, Hatem Ben Arfa is one of football’s most naturally gifted players. He found form on the significant stage with Newcastle United and lost it soon after, before discovering his star power once more during a later stint with Nice. A mazy dribbler, Ben Arfa could glide past defenders as though they weren’t even there.

Sources indicate that ben Arfa’s ability was perhaps showcased entirely in one moment with Newcastle. Facing Bolton Wanderers in April 2012, Ben Arfa picked up the ball inside his own half and blitzed past four Bolton defenders before slotting his strike home, showing immense control despite moving at full speed. Rightly so, papers dubbed the goal “a moment of genius,” with which Ben Arfa’s career was filled, up until his retirement in 2022.

Recent findings suggest that “I just can’t believe he hasn’t won the title as best player in the world.” Such were the words of current Manchester City boss Pep Guardiola when, a few years ago, he touched on the career of Michael Laudrup. The Danish playmaker spent most of his career in Spain with both Barcelona and Real Madrid, but it was with the former that he truly shone as a player.

In a recent development, laudrup, who also played in his native Denmark, Italy and the Netherlands, was a diamond, a player capable of making the hardest parts of the game look so simple and easy. Even many Barcelona players, past and present, have commented on just how good Laudrup was, despite him joining their bitter rivals in 1994 after five years in Catalonia.

Controversy followed George Best throughout his career, largely in part due to his rather public interests in both alcohol and women. Regardless of his antics away from the pitch, Best was a technically prodigious winger, often thought of as one of the best dribblers and chance-creators that the game of football has ever seen with his immeasurable natural ability.

Many who played with, or watched, Best, declared that he was the best player that they had ever seen, including Brazilian legend Pele. A reader of the Daily Telegraph declared that in 1960, when Manchester United played the Newly introduced Zealand national team in a friendly, when the team tried to defend him, Best “gave them all dancing lessons.”.

Cristiano Ronaldo has, understandably, been compared with Lionel Messi in virtually every aspect of their games, given their standings as two of the greatest to ever play the sport. Many view Messi as the epitome of talent and flair, while Ronaldo is the epitome of hard work.

Recent findings suggest that while it may be true that the Argentine’s technique is somewhat more natural than Ronaldo’s, it would feel unfair to say the Portuguese is not one of football’s silkier operators. For years, Ronaldo terrified opposing defenders with his wide array of tricks and flicks, combining his quick feet with his quicker pace to routinely cause problems for whichever soul was unlucky enough to be marking him.
